pageData.title: Abolitionism and Black Activism
pageData.para1: Organized opposition to slavery in the United States began long before the famous abolitionist campaigns of the 1830s. Northern states had abolished slavery gradually after the Revolution, and free Black communities in cities like Philadelphia, New York, and Boston built churches, schools, and mutual aid societies that became the institutional base of the antislavery struggle. In 1817 the American Colonization Society proposed sending free Black Americans to Africa, a plan many white moderates embraced and most Black leaders flatly rejected as a scheme to strengthen slavery by removing free people of color. Black newspapers, beginning with Freedom's Journal in 1827, answered with a clear demand: immediate emancipation and full rights at home.
pageData.para2: In 1829 David Walker, a free Black clothing dealer in Boston, published his Appeal to the Colored Citizens of the World, a militant call for resistance that circulated secretly in the South and terrified slaveholders. Two years later William Lloyd Garrison launched the Liberator, rejecting gradualism and colonization and demanding immediate, uncompensated emancipation. In 1833 Garrison joined Black and white activists to found the American Anti-Slavery Society. Black abolitionists were never junior partners: Maria Stewart became one of the first American women to lecture publicly on politics, Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became the movement's most powerful orator and author of a bestselling Narrative in 1845, and Sojourner Truth carried antislavery and women's rights together onto the lecture circuit.
pageData.para3: Abolitionists flooded Congress with antislavery petitions until the House adopted the gag rule in 1836, automatically tabling them; former president John Quincy Adams fought the rule for eight years until it was repealed. The movement faced mob violence, including the 1837 murder of the antislavery editor Elijah Lovejoy in Illinois. Politically, abolitionists formed the Liberty Party in 1840 and later fed into the Free Soil and Republican coalitions. Black activists organized through a national convention movement, pressed for school integration in northern cities, and sustained the escape networks described on the Underground Railroad page.
pageData.para4: The movement's pressure helped make slavery the central question of national politics, and the Civil War turned its core demand into law: the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 and the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865, both covered on their own pages. Abolitionists then fought for citizenship, suffrage, and education during Reconstruction. When those gains were rolled back, veterans of the movement and their descendants carried the activism into new organizations in the early twentieth century, keeping the demand for equal citizenship alive into the era of the NAACP.

pageData.title: The Underground Railroad and Fugitive Slave Laws
pageData.para1: The Underground Railroad was not a railroad and was never underground: it was a loose, secret network of Black and white Americans who helped enslaved people escape to freedom. Escape was as old as slavery itself, but by the 1830s an organized system of routes, safe houses called stations, and guides known as conductors stretched from the slave states to the northern free states and across the border into Canada, where slavery had been abolished. No central organization ran it; local networks, often anchored in Black communities and Quaker settlements, acted on their own initiative at great personal risk.
pageData.para2: Federal law stood against them. The Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 authorized owners to seize escaped people in free states, and the far harsher Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, part of the Compromise of 1850, created special commissioners, denied accused fugitives a jury trial or the right to testify, and punished anyone who helped them. Free Black northerners were kidnapped into slavery under its provisions, and northern states answered with personal liberty laws that obstructed slave catchers. The 1850 law made every northern community a potential hunting ground and pushed the escape line all the way to Canada.
pageData.para3: The network's most famous conductor, Harriet Tubman, escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and returned south some thirteen times to lead out roughly seventy people, including her own family, without losing a single passenger. Levi and Catharine Coffin in Indiana sheltered more than two thousand fugitives over two decades. Vigilance committees in Philadelphia and other cities, led largely by Black activists such as William Still, coordinated arrivals, raised money, and recorded the stories of those who passed through. Freedom seekers also fled to Spanish Florida, to Mexico, and to the Caribbean, following whatever route led out of bondage.
pageData.para4: Estimates vary, but tens of thousands of enslaved people escaped between 1830 and 1860, each departure a small act of war against the slave system. The 1850 law's cruelties radicalized northern opinion; Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), written in its shadow, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. The network's collaborators carried their experience into the abolitionist movement and wartime service. The Underground Railroad's history, recovered by scholars and preserved at sites now administered by the National Park Service, remains a testament to organized resistance by ordinary people against an unjust law.

pageData.title: Seneca Falls and the Early Women's Rights Movement
pageData.para1: In the early nineteenth century, American women lived under the common-law doctrine of coverture: a married woman's legal identity was absorbed into her husband's. She could not vote, sign contracts, sue, or control her own earnings or property, and colleges and the professions were closed to her. The reform movements of the era opened a crack in that wall. Women did much of the work in temperance, charitable, and antislavery societies, and in doing so they discovered both their own organizing power and the contradiction of demanding freedom for the enslaved while being denied basic rights themselves.
pageData.para2: The immediate spark came at the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London in 1840, where the women chosen as American delegates, including Lucretia Mott, were refused seats because of their sex; Elizabeth Cady Stanton, in London with her delegate husband, was likewise allowed only to listen, not to participate. Eight years later the two women organized a convention at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, on July 19-20, 1848. About three hundred people attended, including the abolitionist Frederick Douglass. The convention adopted a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence, listing men's repeated injuries and usurpations toward women. Its most radical resolution, demanding the vote, passed only after Douglass rose to defend it.
pageData.para3: Seneca Falls was the beginning, not the whole movement. From 1850, national women's rights conventions met nearly every year, and activists won concrete legal gains, including New York's Married Women's Property Acts of 1848 and 1860, which let wives own property and keep their earnings. New institutions opened: Oberlin had admitted women since 1837, and Mount Holyoke Female Seminary, founded by Mary Lyon in 1837, offered serious higher education. The Civil War suspended the conventions, and the movement split afterward over whether to support the Fifteenth Amendment, which enfranchised Black men but not women.
pageData.para4: In 1869 Stanton and Susan B. Anthony formed the National Woman Suffrage Association while rivals founded the American Woman Suffrage Association; the two merged in 1890 as the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Meanwhile the West led: Wyoming Territory granted women the vote in 1869, followed by Utah, Colorado, and Idaho before 1900. Generations of petitioning, state referenda, and organizing finally produced the Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, which forbade denying the vote on account of sex, seventy-two years after the first resolution at Seneca Falls.

pageData.title: Manifest Destiny, the Oregon Trail and Western Settlement
pageData.para1: In 1845 the journalist John L. O'Sullivan gave a name to a widespread conviction when he wrote of America's manifest destiny to overspread the continent. The idea mixed genuine beliefs about liberty and opportunity with a claim that the United States was entitled to the lands of Indigenous nations and Mexico. Expansion was already under way: American traders had followed the Santa Fe Trail since the 1820s, fur trappers had mapped the Rockies, and missionaries and settlers were filtering into the Oregon Country, which Britain and the United States occupied jointly. In the 1840s expansion became national policy, driving the annexation of Texas, the war with Mexico, and the partition of Oregon.
pageData.para2: The Oregon Trail was the great corridor of that migration. From Independence, Missouri, the trail ran some two thousand miles across the plains, along the Platte River, through South Pass in the Rockies, and down the Snake and Columbia rivers to the Willamette Valley. The first large wagon trains rolled in 1843, and over the following two decades an estimated three hundred thousand emigrants made the journey, walking beside their wagons for five or six months. Cholera killed far more travelers than any other cause, and accidents, exhaustion, and disputes broke many parties; the Donner Party, California-bound emigrants who left the main trail for the Hastings Cutoff and were trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in 1846-1847, became the era's most infamous disaster. From 1847, Mormon emigrants followed a parallel route to their new settlement in the Great Salt Lake Valley.
pageData.para3: The trails crossed the homelands of the Pawnee, Cheyenne, Lakota, Shoshone, Cayuse, and many other nations, whose economies depended on the buffalo herds and river valleys the emigrants disrupted. Many Indigenous people initially traded with or guided the wagon trains, but the traffic brought disease, depleted game, and mounting conflict. The killing of the missionaries Marcus and Narcissa Whitman by Cayuse warriors in 1847, after a measles epidemic devastated their people, sparked the Cayuse War and hardened demands for military control of the corridor. Treaties such as the 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie attempted to fix tribal territories and safe passage, but settlement steadily overran the agreements.
pageData.para4: By 1846 the Oregon Treaty had divided the region with Britain at the forty-ninth parallel, and Oregon entered the Union as a state in 1859. The overland migration populated the Pacific coast, tightened the bond between East and West, and created the demand for the transcontinental railroad that replaced the wagon trains after 1869. For the Indigenous nations of the plains and Northwest, the trail era opened a generation of dispossession and war, a story continued on the Plains Indian Wars page.

pageData.title: The California Gold Rush
pageData.para1: On January 24, 1848, a carpenter named James W. Marshall found flakes of gold in the tailrace of a sawmill he was building for John Sutter on the American River in California. Days later the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transferred California from Mexico to the United States, so the greatest gold discovery in American history passed almost immediately into American hands. Local workers deserted the fields and shops for the diggings, and by December President Polk confirmed the discoveries to Congress. In 1849 the world rushed in: some eighty thousand people reached California that year alone, by sea around Cape Horn or across Panama, and by the overland trails.
pageData.para2: The forty-niners came from every continent: Americans from the eastern states, Mexicans and Chileans with mining experience, Chinese from Guangdong, Europeans, Australians, and Hawaiians. San Francisco exploded from a village of about a thousand people into a chaotic city of tens of thousands, with canvas tents, astronomical prices, and fortunes made more reliably by merchants than by miners. California's non-Indigenous population reached perhaps three hundred thousand within five years. Mining camps sprang up across the Sierra Nevada foothills, rough male societies governed by improvised miners' codes, where a good claim could yield astonishing sums and most men found barely enough to stay.
pageData.para3: The easy gold did not last. Individual placer mining gave way within a decade to capital-intensive operations: hydraulic mining that blasted entire hillsides with water cannon, and deep quartz mining financed by companies. The environmental damage was severe, clogging rivers with debris that flooded farms downstream until courts curbed hydraulic mining in the 1880s. The human costs fell hardest on others: California's Indigenous peoples suffered violence, enslavement under legal cover, and a catastrophic population collapse, while a Foreign Miners' Tax of 1850 and repeated violence drove out many Mexican and Chinese miners. Discrimination against the Chinese, continued on the Chinese Exclusion page, began in the goldfields.
pageData.para4: The rush remade the nation. Gold poured into the American and world economies, California entered the Union as a free state in 1850 as part of the Compromise of 1850, and the new wealth financed banks, steamship lines, and eventually the western end of the transcontinental railroad. San Francisco became the Pacific coast's great city, and agriculture flourished as mining declined. The gold rush also fixed an enduring image in American culture: the idea of the West as a place where a lucky break could remake a life, and the reality that such booms enriched few while displacing many.

pageData.title: The Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850
pageData.para1: In 1819 the territory of Missouri applied for statehood as a slave state, and the House of Representatives, where the free states held a majority, tried to bar the further spread of slavery there. The Senate, evenly divided between eleven slave and eleven free states, refused. After a year of deadlock, Congress settled the first great sectional crisis in 1820: Missouri entered as a slave state, Maine was carved from Massachusetts as a free state to preserve the balance, and slavery was prohibited in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase territory north of the line of 36 degrees 30 minutes, Missouri's southern border. The aging Thomas Jefferson called the dispute a fire bell in the night, a warning of worse to come.
pageData.para2: The Missouri Compromise held for three decades because it rested on a simple bargain: the Senate stayed balanced, and the vast western lands were divided in advance between freedom and slavery. But the bargain contained a fatal weakness. It settled only the Louisiana Purchase, and it depended on both sections accepting limits on slavery's expansion. Southern leaders increasingly rejected any limit as a threat to their political power, while northern opinion slowly turned against the extension of slavery on principle.
pageData.para3: The war with Mexico shattered the arrangement. The Wilmot Proviso of 1846, repeatedly passed by the House and blocked in the Senate, demanded that slavery be excluded from any territory taken from Mexico. When gold rush California sought admission as a free state in 1849, the sectional balance collapsed. Henry Clay proposed a grand settlement, and after his omnibus bill failed, Stephen Douglas steered the measures through separately in 1850: California entered free; the territories of New Mexico and Utah were organized without a slavery prohibition; Texas surrendered its western claims for ten million dollars; the slave trade, though not slavery, was abolished in the District of Columbia; and a drastic new Fugitive Slave Act, described on the Underground Railroad page, put federal power behind the capture of escaped people.
pageData.para4: The Compromise of 1850 bought the Union a decade, but its fugitive slave law poisoned northern opinion and its silence on the old 36-30 line invited new bargains. In 1854 the Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri line outright, and in 1857 the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision declared the original compromise unconstitutional. What two generations of statesmen had built to hold the Union together, the next generation tore apart within seven years.

pageData.title: The Kansas-Nebraska Act and Bleeding Kansas
pageData.para1: In 1854 Senator Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois wanted to organize the territories of Kansas and Nebraska, partly to clear the way for a transcontinental railroad through his home state. To win southern votes, his Kansas-Nebraska Act declared that the settlers of each territory would decide the slavery question themselves, a formula he called popular sovereignty. Because both territories lay north of the 36-30 line, the act repealed the Missouri Compromise's thirty-four-year-old ban on slavery there. Northern reaction was ferocious: the act shattered the Whig Party, and opponents of slavery's extension founded the Republican Party that same year.
pageData.para2: Popular sovereignty turned Kansas into a prize to be won by settlement. Northern emigrant aid societies sent free-state colonists with rifles and supplies, while proslavery Missourians, derided as border ruffians, crossed the line to vote illegally and intimidate their neighbors. Proslavery forces stole the territorial elections of 1854 and 1855, and Kansas soon had two rival governments: a proslavery legislature at Lecompton and a free-state government at Topeka. Both appealed to a divided Washington, where President Pierce recognized the proslavery regime.
pageData.para3: Politics gave way to war. In May 1856 a proslavery posse sacked the free-state town of Lawrence. Days later the abolitionist John Brown, convinced that only violence could answer violence, led a band that dragged five proslavery settlers from their cabins at Pottawatomie Creek and hacked them to death. Guerrilla raids, ambushes, and arson spread across the territory over the next two years, killing more than fifty people in all. In 1857 the proslavery convention at Lecompton drafted a constitution protecting slavery and rigged the referendum on it; Congress refused to accept it, and Kansas finally entered the Union as a free state in January 1861, as the South was already seceding.
pageData.para4: Bleeding Kansas was a rehearsal for the Civil War, fought over the same question with the same passions. Its violence reached even the Senate floor, where in 1856 Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts nearly to death with a cane after an antislavery speech. The crisis proved that popular sovereignty could not settle the slavery question peacefully, destroyed the last national party capable of bridging the sections, and made the new Republican Party, and Abraham Lincoln, the vehicle of northern resolve.

pageData.title: Dred Scott, John Brown and the Crisis of the Union
pageData.para1: Dred Scott was an enslaved man whose owner, an army surgeon, had taken him for years into the free state of Illinois and the free territory of Wisconsin. In 1846 Scott sued for his freedom in Missouri, arguing that residence on free soil had made him free. After eleven years of litigation, the Supreme Court decided his case in March 1857. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney's opinion held that Black Americans, whether enslaved or free, were not and could not become citizens of the United States, and that Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories, making the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional. Instead of settling the slavery question, the decision wiped out the legal basis for compromise and delighted the South while horrifying the North.
pageData.para2: Northern reaction fused fear and fury. Republicans charged that a slave power conspiracy meant to nationalize slavery, and the new party's ranks swelled. The ruling hung over the 1858 Illinois Senate race, where Abraham Lincoln pressed Stephen Douglas to explain how popular sovereignty could survive a decision forbidding any ban on slavery. Douglas answered with his Freeport Doctrine, arguing that territorial settlers could still exclude slavery by refusing to protect it, a position that saved his Senate seat but split the Democratic Party between North and South.
pageData.para3: John Brown chose a shorter road. Fresh from the guerrilla war in Kansas, the veteran abolitionist planned to seize the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, arm the enslaved people of the surrounding country, and build a mountain stronghold of freedom. On the night of October 16, 1859, Brown and twenty-one followers, Black and white, captured the arsenal. Local militia and then United States Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee stormed the engine house where Brown made his stand. Ten of his men were killed and Brown was captured, tried by the state of Virginia for treason, and hanged on December 2, 1859, conducting himself with a calm dignity that impressed even his enemies.
pageData.para4: Across the North, church bells tolled for Brown and writers like Thoreau and Emerson hailed him as a martyr; across the South, his raid confirmed that abolitionists meant to loose a slave rebellion, and militias drilled for the conflict to come. The next year the Democratic Party broke apart, the Republican Abraham Lincoln won the presidency without a single southern electoral vote, and South Carolina led the Deep South out of the Union. The crisis that compromise could no longer contain became the Civil War, covered on its own page.

pageData.title: The American Civil War: Causes, Campaigns and Union Victory
pageData.para1: The Civil War grew out of the sectional conflict over slavery's expansion that compromise after compromise had failed to settle. When Abraham Lincoln, pledged to stop slavery's spread, won the presidency in November 1860, South Carolina seceded in December, followed by six more Deep South states that formed the Confederate States of America under President Jefferson Davis. On April 12, 1861, Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbor, Lincoln called for seventy-five thousand volunteers to suppress the rebellion, and four more slave states, including Virginia, joined the Confederacy. Both sides expected a short war; both were wrong.
pageData.para2: The war in the East became a grinding contest between the Union Army of the Potomac and Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia. After the Union disaster at First Bull Run in July 1861, a series of cautious Union generals failed to exploit their advantages. Lee repelled George McClellan's drive on Richmond in 1862, invaded the North, and was stopped at Antietam that September, the bloodiest single day in American history. Lee won brilliant victories at Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville, but his second invasion ended at Gettysburg in July 1863, the war's turning point in the East.
pageData.para3: In the West, Ulysses S. Grant opened the war's decisive theater. His captures of Forts Henry and Donelson in 1862 split Confederate defenses, and after the terrible battle of Shiloh his army drove south. The surrender of Vicksburg on July 4, 1863, followed by Port Hudson's five days later, gave the Union control of the Mississippi River and cut the Confederacy in two, while a Union naval blockade slowly strangled southern trade. In 1864 Lincoln made Grant general in chief: Grant hammered Lee in Virginia while William T. Sherman took Atlanta and marched across Georgia to the sea, destroying the South's capacity and will to fight. Lee, cornered and starving, surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on April 9, 1865.
pageData.para4: The Union won because of its crushing advantages in population, industry, railroads, and finance, because its navy commanded the seas and rivers, because Lincoln's leadership held the northern coalition together, and because emancipation, covered on its own page, turned the war into a fight the Confederacy could not win diplomatically or morally. The war cost some 620,000 soldiers' lives, more than all other American wars combined to that date. It destroyed slavery, settled secession forever, and created a more powerful federal government, leaving the unresolved work of freedom to Reconstruction.

pageData.title: Emancipation and African Americans in the Civil War
pageData.para1: The Civil War did not begin as a war to end slavery: Lincoln's stated purpose was to preserve the Union, and he moved carefully to hold the loyal slave states of the border. The enslaved themselves forced the issue. From the war's first weeks, freedom seekers fled to Union lines, and in May 1861 General Benjamin Butler refused to return them, declaring them contraband of war. As Union armies advanced, hundreds of thousands liberated themselves, laboring for the Union and draining the Confederacy's workforce. Congress responded with Confiscation Acts in 1861 and 1862 that freed enslaved people used by the rebellion.
pageData.para2: On September 22, 1862, after the Union victory at Antietam, Lincoln issued a preliminary warning, and on January 1, 1863, he signed the Emancipation Proclamation. It declared free all enslaved people in the states then in rebellion, a wartime measure under his powers as commander in chief that exempted the border states and occupied areas. Its practical reach grew only as Union armies advanced, but it transformed the war: every Union advance now carried freedom, the Confederacy could no longer hope for British or French intervention on behalf of slavery, and the Union cause became openly a fight against bondage.
pageData.para3: The Proclamation also opened the Army to Black men, who had been barred from service at the war's start. By the end of the war roughly 180,000 Black soldiers had served in the United States Colored Troops, about a tenth of the Union army, with thousands more Black sailors in the navy. The 54th Massachusetts Infantry's assault on Fort Wagner in July 1863 proved Black soldiers' courage to a skeptical public; Black troops fought at Milliken's Bend, Port Hudson, and the Crater at Petersburg, and some three hundred were massacred after surrendering at Fort Pillow in 1864. They fought for equal pay as well, receiving less than white soldiers until Congress equalized pay in 1864.
pageData.para4: Because the Proclamation rested on war powers, abolitionists pushed for a constitutional guarantee. The Thirteenth Amendment, abolishing slavery everywhere in the United States, passed Congress in January 1865 and was ratified that December. In all, about four million Americans walked out of slavery, the largest emancipation in the Atlantic world. Freedom's first fruits, family reunification, schools, churches, and political organizing, defined the Reconstruction struggles covered on the following pages, and the memory of emancipation, celebrated as Juneteenth from the last Texas freedpeople's liberation in June 1865, endured for generations.

pageData.title: The Civil War Home Front: Mobilization, Women and Dissent
pageData.para1: The Civil War demanded more from civilians than any previous American conflict. Both governments raised armies first by volunteers, then by conscription: the Confederacy adopted a draft in 1862 and the Union followed in 1863. The Union draft allowed the wealthy to hire substitutes or pay a commutation fee, and in July 1863 working-class New Yorkers, many of them Irish immigrants, exploded in four days of draft riots, attacking draft offices and murdering Black residents before troops from Gettysburg restored order. To pay for the war the Union printed greenback paper money, sold bonds to ordinary citizens through the banker Jay Cooke, and levied the first federal income tax, while a Republican Congress passed the Homestead Act, the Morrill land-grant college act, and the Pacific Railway Act, all in 1862.
pageData.para2: Women kept both societies running. They took over farms, plantations, and family businesses, worked in arsenals and government offices, and served by the thousands as nurses, work once thought unsuitable for women. Dorothea Dix became superintendent of Union army nurses, Clara Barton carried supplies to the front lines and later founded the American Red Cross, and the United States Sanitary Commission, a civilian relief organization run largely by women volunteers, raised millions of dollars and policed camp hygiene. In the Confederacy, women organized relief societies and worked in hospitals such as Richmond's vast Chimborazo.
pageData.para3: Both governments faced dissent. In the North, Peace Democrats, branded Copperheads, denounced the war and emancipation; their leader Clement Vallandigham was arrested and banished to the Confederacy in 1863 after Lincoln's administration suspended the writ of habeas corpus. In the South, food shortages and inflation sparked bread riots in Richmond and other cities in 1863, desertion drained the army, and poor farmers grumbled that it was a rich man's war and a poor man's fight, resenting the draft exemption for large slaveholders.
pageData.para4: The home front decided the war as surely as the battlefields. The Union's ability to finance, equip, and replace its armies grew stronger every year, while the Confederacy's economy collapsed under blockade and inflation. The war also permanently enlarged the federal government's role in the economy and daily life, and it moved women into public and paid work on a new scale, experience many carried into the postwar suffrage and reform movements.

pageData.title: Civil War Medicine and Military Hospitals
pageData.para1: The Civil War was fought before germ theory, and disease killed roughly two soldiers for every one who died of wounds. Crowded camps bred dysentery, typhoid, malaria, measles, and pneumonia, and armies on the march carried their epidemics with them. A wound to the abdomen or chest was usually fatal; the slow-moving Minié ball shattered bone, and infection followed surgery as a matter of course. At the war's start the tiny prewar medical corps was overwhelmed, and the care of millions of volunteers had to be invented as the war went on.
pageData.para2: Out of that improvisation came lasting institutions. The United States Sanitary Commission, a civilian organization, inspected camps, supplied nurses and bandages, and pressed the army on hygiene. Surgeon Jonathan Letterman, medical director of the Army of the Potomac, built an organized ambulance corps and a triage system of field dressing stations, division hospitals, and general hospitals that treated casualties by severity rather than rank, the ancestor of modern military medicine. Huge pavilion-style general hospitals, such as Satterlee in Philadelphia and Chimborazo in Richmond, housed thousands of patients in airy wards that reduced cross-infection.
pageData.para3: Surgeons worked at brutal speed under fire, but anesthesia was standard: chloroform or ether was used in the great majority of operations, and the war's image of men biting bullets through conscious amputations is largely myth. Amputation was the common answer to shattered limbs, performed in minutes by experienced hands. Women served in the wards despite official resistance, Clara Barton and the volunteer nurses Dorothea Dix recruited among them, and the writer Walt Whitman spent years comforting the wounded in Washington hospitals. Armies on both sides kept medical records that filled the six-volume Medical and Surgical History of the War of the Rebellion.
pageData.para4: The war professionalized American medicine. It trained thousands of surgeons, created a nursing profession that women led after the war, demonstrated the value of sanitation and hospital design, and left a system of veterans' care and pensions that became a major federal obligation. The ambulance, triage, and evacuation systems Letterman sketched in 1862 still underlie military and emergency medicine. That the war's lessons spread so slowly into civilian public health was the era's tragedy; that they were learned at all was its legacy.

pageData.title: Reconstruction and the Thirteenth, Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments
pageData.para1: When the Civil War ended in 1865, the United States faced three enormous questions: how to readmit the defeated southern states, what place four million freedpeople would hold in the nation, and who would decide. Lincoln had proposed lenient readmission when a tenth of a state's voters swore loyalty, but his assassination in April 1865 left President Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee Democrat, in charge. Johnson pardoned most Confederates and allowed southern legislatures to enact the Black Codes, laws that restricted freedpeople's movement, labor, and rights so tightly they amounted to slavery in new dress.
pageData.para2: Congressional Republicans, outraged by the Black Codes and by southern violence, seized control of Reconstruction. They passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 over Johnson's veto, and in the Reconstruction Acts of 1867 they divided the South into five military districts and required new state constitutions providing Black male suffrage before readmission. Johnson's resistance to Congress led the House to impeach him in 1868; the Senate acquitted him by one vote. Under military protection, southern voters, Black and white, elected conventions that wrote the region's most democratic constitutions to date, and every former Confederate state was readmitted by 1870.
pageData.para3: At the movement's heart stood three constitutional amendments. The Thirteenth, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery. The Fourteenth, ratified in 1868, made citizens of all persons born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction, overturning Dred Scott, and guaranteed equal protection of the laws. The Fifteenth, ratified in 1870, forbade denying the vote on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude. The Freedmen's Bureau, covered on its own page, worked alongside these changes to aid the transition from slavery to freedom.
pageData.para4: Congressional Reconstruction transformed the South's politics and public life for a decade, described on the Black Political Participation page, before violence, exhaustion, and the Compromise of 1877 ended it, as the End of Reconstruction page recounts. Their promises of racial equality faced sustained resistance and uneven enforcement. The amendments nevertheless remained in the Constitution, the reason Reconstruction is often called America's unfinished revolution.

pageData.title: The Freedmen's Bureau and the Struggle for Land and Education
pageData.para1: In March 1865, weeks before the Civil War ended, Congress created the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, known as the Freedmen's Bureau, to manage the transition from slavery to freedom in the devastated South. Under General Oliver O. Howard, the Bureau fed the hungry, white and Black alike, ran hospitals, reunited families separated by slavery, legalized marriages performed under bondage, and supervised labor contracts between freedpeople and planters. It was the first large federal social welfare agency in American history, and in its peak years it operated in every former Confederate state with only about nine hundred agents.
pageData.para2: The Bureau's greatest success was education. Freedpeople, long forbidden to learn to read, demanded schools with extraordinary determination, organizing their own classes and raising money from poverty itself. Working with northern missionary and freedmen's aid societies and with Black communities, the Bureau helped establish thousands of schools serving hundreds of thousands of students. It also supported new colleges for Black students, including Howard University in Washington, Fisk in Nashville, and Hampton in Virginia, institutions that educated Black teachers and leaders for generations.
pageData.para3: The central question was land. In January 1865 General William T. Sherman's Field Order 15 had set aside coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia for freed families, forty-acre plots that gave rise to the phrase forty acres and a mule. The Bureau held hundreds of thousands of acres of abandoned and confiscated land that freedpeople hoped to receive. President Johnson ordered nearly all of it restored to former owners in 1865, and Congress never enacted land redistribution. Without land, most freedpeople had to work for their former enslavers, and the Bureau's supervised labor contracts evolved into sharecropping and crop liens that trapped Black farmers in debt for generations.
pageData.para4: The Bureau fought constant opposition: President Johnson vetoed its renewal before Congress overrode him, southern whites denounced it, and it was always underfunded and understaffed. Congress let it expire in 1872. Its relief work saved countless lives and its courts offered freedpeople a rare forum for justice, but its failure on land shaped the South's poverty and racial hierarchy for a century. The schools and colleges it planted were its most durable monument, anchoring Black education through the era of segregation.

pageData.title: Black Political Participation during Reconstruction
pageData.para1: Reconstruction made citizens and voters of men who had been property. Under the Reconstruction Acts of 1867 and the Fifteenth Amendment, Black men registered to vote across the South, forming a majority of the electorate in South Carolina, Mississippi, and Louisiana. Organized through Union Leagues, churches, and Republican clubs, they built a biracial coalition with northern transplants and southern white Republicans that elected new state governments charged with rebuilding the region.
pageData.para2: Roughly two thousand Black men held public office during Reconstruction, at every level from local school boards to the United States Senate. Hiram Revels of Mississippi took the Senate seat once held by Jefferson Davis in 1870, and Blanche Kelso Bruce, also of Mississippi, served a full term. Sixteen Black men served in the House of Representatives, including Robert Smalls of South Carolina, who had delivered a Confederate ship to the Union navy. P. B. S. Pinchback briefly served as acting governor of Louisiana, and Black legislators sat in every southern statehouse; South Carolina's lower house had a Black majority. Contrary to later caricature, these officeholders were often literate, experienced community leaders, and their governments were no more corrupt than others of the era.
pageData.para3: The Reconstruction governments' achievements were real. They created the South's first public school systems for Black and white children, founded state universities and hospitals, reformed taxation and the courts, and rebuilt railroads and levees destroyed by war. Black communities built institutions of their own: independent churches became the region's Black civic centers, new colleges trained teachers, and Black newspapers and fraternal societies tied communities together.
pageData.para4: Black political power was destroyed by violence. The Ku Klux Klan and allied paramilitary groups like the White League and the Red Shirts assassinated officeholders, whipped teachers, and massacred Black voters at Colfax, Louisiana, in 1873 and Hamburg, South Carolina, in 1876. Federal enforcement laws of 1870-1871 broke the first Klan, but northern will faded, and after 1877 the last Republican governments fell. Black southerners voted and held some offices into the 1890s, when disfranchisement ended the experiment, described on the End of Reconstruction page.

pageData.title: The End of Reconstruction and the Rise of Jim Crow
pageData.para1: Reconstruction died of exhaustion, violence, and political retreat. Northern voters wearied of southern conflict after the Panic of 1873 plunged the country into depression, and Democrats, calling themselves redeemers, recaptured southern state governments one by one through a combination of economic pressure, propaganda, and paramilitary terror against Black voters. Federal enforcement waned as the Supreme Court narrowed the reach of the Reconstruction amendments in cases like the Slaughterhouse Cases of 1873 and United States v. Cruikshank in 1876.
pageData.para2: The disputed presidential election of 1876 finished the process. Democrat Samuel Tilden won the popular vote, but the electoral votes of three southern states were contested. In the informal Compromise of 1877, Democrats accepted the Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president in exchange for the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South. The remaining Republican governments collapsed, and Black southerners were left to face the redeemers alone.
pageData.para3: Over the following generation the southern states built the Jim Crow system. Laws segregated railroads, schools, hospitals, and public spaces, and in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 the Supreme Court upheld segregation as separate but equal. Beginning with Mississippi in 1890, states stripped Black men of the vote through poll taxes, literacy tests, understanding clauses, and white primaries, wiping out the Fifteenth Amendment's promise. Lynching and racial terror enforced the order - between 1889 and 1918 alone, lynching mobs killed 3,224 people, 2,522 of them Black - and convict leasing returned thousands to forced labor.
pageData.para4: Black Americans resisted from the start. The journalist Ida B. Wells risked her life documenting lynching in the 1890s, and communities defended schools, churches, and businesses. As conditions worsened, hundreds of thousands left the South in the Great Migration that swelled after 1915, and racial violence followed them north, from the Red Summer of 1919 to the destruction of Tulsa's Black Wall Street in 1921. The revived Ku Klux Klan of the 1910s and 1920s showed how deeply Jim Crow's logic had spread beyond the South by 1924.

pageData.title: The Transcontinental Railroad and Chinese Railroad Workers
pageData.para1: For decades Americans dreamed of a railroad binding the Pacific coast to the East. The Pacific Railway Acts of 1862 and 1864 made it a national project: the federal government chartered two companies, granted them enormous land subsidies along the route, and loaned them bonds for every mile of track. The Union Pacific built westward from Omaha, Nebraska, largely with Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans, while the Central Pacific, the creation of Sacramento merchants Leland Stanford, Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins, and Charles Crocker, tackled the far harder task eastward over the Sierra Nevada.
pageData.para2: The Central Pacific's workforce became mostly Chinese. Skeptical at first, Crocker hired Chinese laborers in 1865, and they proved so capable that the company recruited them by the thousands, eventually about twelve thousand men, some ninety percent of its workforce. They bored fifteen tunnels through Sierra granite with hand drills and black-powder blasting, one of the most dangerous jobs on the line, and endured avalanches that buried entire camps. They were paid less than white workers and had to buy their own food and lodging. In June 1867 several thousand Chinese tracklayers struck for higher pay and shorter hours, a remarkable act of labor solidarity that Crocker broke by cutting off their food supplies.
pageData.para3: On May 10, 1869, the two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, where Leland Stanford drove a ceremonial golden spike and telegraph wires carried the news to a celebrating nation. A journey from New York to San Francisco that had taken months by sea or wagon now took about a week. The Chinese workers who made it possible were pointedly absent from the famous photographs, and within a generation the country they had helped bind together barred their countrymen, as the Chinese Exclusion page recounts.
pageData.para4: The railroads transformed the West: they carried settlers, cattle, wheat, and minerals to market, created national networks of time and trade, and made the railroad corporations the nation's first big businesses, with the corruption to match, including the Credit Mobilier scandal that reached Congress in 1872. By 1900 five transcontinental lines crossed the country. The project stands as both an engineering triumph and a parable of the era: public generosity, private fortune, and immigrant labor whose contribution was long written out of the story.

pageData.title: Immigration, Ellis Island and Urban America
pageData.para1: In the mass-migration era from 1880 to 1924, more than twenty-five million immigrants came to the United States. The first postwar wave still came largely from Ireland, Germany, Britain, and Scandinavia; after 1880 the balance shifted to southern and eastern Europe: Italians, Poles, Greeks, Hungarians, and some two million Jews fleeing the Russian Empire's pogroms. They came for wages a European farm could never pay, for land, for family members who had gone before, and to escape conscription and persecution. Steamships cut the Atlantic crossing to about two weeks, and labor agents and letters home guided the stream.
pageData.para2: From 1892 the federal government funneled the flood through Ellis Island in New York Harbor, where over twelve million arrivals were processed between 1892 and 1924 alone. First- and second-class passengers were waved through aboard ship; steerage passengers faced the registry hall, where inspectors checked for disease, disability, and signs of contract labor, and where about a fifth were set aside for further inspection while roughly two percent were excluded outright and sent back, sometimes splitting families. On the Pacific coast, Chinese arrivals faced a different regime entirely, described on the Chinese Exclusion page, and from 1910 the Angel Island station detained Asian immigrants for weeks of interrogation.
pageData.para3: Most immigrants settled in cities, and the cities strained to hold them. New York's Lower East Side became the emblem of that crowding, its families packed into dumbbell tenements where tuberculosis and fire were constant companions. Immigrants dug the subways, sewed the garments, and manned the steel mills and stockyards, and their neighborhoods built an infrastructure of mutual aid: synagogues and parishes, foreign-language newspapers, fraternal societies, and political machines like Tammany Hall that traded services for votes. Nativism grew with the numbers: the American Protective Association attacked Catholics in the 1880s, and the Immigration Restriction League campaigned for a literacy test, enacted over vetoes in 1917.
pageData.para4: The newcomers remade American labor, cities, food, music, and politics, and their children filled the common schools and the armies of 1917. But restriction won the argument of the era: the Emergency Quota Act of 1921 and the Immigration Act of 1924 slammed the gates with national-origins quotas designed to favor northwestern Europe, ending the great age of immigration.

pageData.title: Chinese Exclusion and Anti-Asian Discrimination
pageData.para1: Chinese immigrants first came to California in large numbers for the gold rush, and they stayed to build the transcontinental railroad, reclaim farmland, and work in factories and laundries. They met organized hostility from the start: miners' taxes aimed at foreigners, testimony barred in court, segregated schools in San Francisco, and periodic mob violence. After the railroad's completion, economic depression fed the scapegoating. Denis Kearney's Workingmen's Party rallied San Francisco sandlots under the cry The Chinese Must Go, and a mob sacked the city's Chinatown in 1877.
pageData.para2: In 1882 Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act, suspending the immigration of Chinese laborers for ten years and barring Chinese residents from citizenship. It was the first major American law to exclude a nationality by name. The Geary Act of 1892 renewed exclusion and required Chinese residents to carry certificates of residence on pain of deportation; in 1902 exclusion was made indefinite, and in 1917 Congress added an Asiatic Barred Zone covering most of Asia. On the Pacific coast, the Angel Island station, opened in 1910, detained arriving Chinese for weeks or months of interrogation. The Immigration Act of 1924 folded Asian exclusion into the new national-origins quota system.
pageData.para3: Chinese Americans fought back through the courts and their own institutions. In Yick Wo v. Hopkins (1886) the Supreme Court struck down San Francisco's discriminatory laundry licensing as a violation of equal protection. In United States v. Wong Kim Ark (1898) the Court confirmed that children born in the United States to Chinese parents were birthright citizens under the Fourteenth Amendment. Community associations, the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association above all, funded lawsuits and defended residents, and after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake destroyed the city's records, thousands established citizenship claims through the paper sons system.
pageData.para4: The exclusion era was written in blood as well as law: white miners murdered twenty-eight Chinese coal miners at Rock Springs, Wyoming, in 1885, and Chinese communities were expelled from Tacoma and Seattle in 1885-1886. Exclusion split families for generations, since wives generally could not join laborer husbands, and it established the template for the racialized immigration restrictions that followed.

pageData.title: The Populist Movement and the Farmers' Revolt
pageData.para1: In the decades after the Civil War, American farmers fed the nation and starved on the proceeds. Grain and cotton prices fell for a generation while railroad freight rates, equipment costs, and interest stayed high. The money supply, tied to gold, shrank behind the growing economy, so every dollar of debt grew heavier each year. On the Great Plains homesteaders mortgaged their farms for seed and machines; in the South, sharecroppers and tenants, Black and white, sank into the crop-lien system, surrendering each year's crop to the furnishing merchant before it was grown. By the 1880s farmers believed, with reason, that railroads, banks, and middlemen owned their labor.
pageData.para2: Farmers organized. The Grange, founded in 1867, spread cooperative stores and won state laws regulating railroad rates that the Supreme Court upheld in Munn v. Illinois in 1877. In the 1880s the Farmers' Alliances, the Northwestern and Southern Alliances and the Colored Farmers' Alliance, enrolled millions, ran cooperatives, and lectured members on finance. When the cooperatives failed against concentrated capital, the Southern Alliance proposed the subtreasury plan, a federal system to store crops and lend against them, and in 1890 the movement issued the Ocala Demands: the subtreasury, the free coinage of silver to expand the money supply, a graduated income tax, direct election of senators, and government ownership of railroads and telegraphs.
pageData.para3: When both old parties refused the program, the Alliance men founded the People's Party, the Populists, in 1891. Their 1892 Omaha Platform declared that the fruits of the toil of millions are boldly stolen to build up colossal fortunes for a few, and their candidate, James B. Weaver, won over a million votes and four western states. After the Panic of 1893 threw millions out of work, the movement surged: Jacob Coxey led an army of the unemployed to Washington in 1894 demanding jobs on public works. In 1896 the Democrats adopted free silver and nominated William Jennings Bryan, who thundered against crucifying mankind on a cross of gold; the Populists fused behind him. Bryan lost to William McKinley, and fusion destroyed the People's Party as an independent force.
pageData.para4: Populism died, but its platform marched on without it. Within two decades the nation adopted the graduated income tax and direct election of senators through the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Amendments in 1913, created the Federal Reserve to manage the currency, regulated railroads more strictly, and legalized much of the cooperative and credit machinery the Alliances had demanded. The farmers' revolt of the 1880s and 1890s was the last great challenge to industrial capitalism from rural America, and much of the Progressive Era state was built on foundations the Populists laid.

pageData.title: Prohibition and the Eighteenth Amendment, 1919-1924
pageData.titleline: Prohibition and the Eighteenth Amendment, 1919-1924 - The History Web
pageData.para1: Prohibition was the culmination of a century of temperance crusading. Reformers had long blamed alcohol for poverty, domestic violence, and political corruption, and organizations like the Woman's Christian Temperance Union and, from 1893, the Anti-Saloon League built a political machine dedicated to destroying the liquor trade. World War I, with its grain shortages and hostility to German-American brewers, gave the drys their opening: the Eighteenth Amendment, banning the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors, was ratified in January 1919, and Congress passed the Volstead Act that October to enforce it. Prohibition took effect in January 1920.
pageData.para2: The dry experiment changed drinking habits but did not end drinking. Saloons closed and alcohol consumption fell at first, especially in rural areas that had supported the law. But in the cities, illegal 'speakeasies' multiplied; within a few years New York City alone counted tens of thousands of them. Homemade 'bathtub gin,' smuggled Canadian whiskey, and medicinal and sacramental exemptions supplied the demand that the law could not suppress.
pageData.para3: Enforcement was starved and outmatched. Congress funded far too few agents to police 18,000 miles of coastline and every city block, and bribery became routine. Bootlegging grew into big business: liquor came over the Canadian border, off 'Rum Row' ships anchored outside the three-mile limit, and out of thousands of illicit stills and breweries. Organized criminal syndicates in the big cities made fortunes from the trade and defended them with bribery and violence, corrupting police, judges, and politicians, while the fashion for hip flasks and cocktails made lawbreaking a kind of urban chic.
pageData.para4: By 1924 the country was already arguing over whether the 'noble experiment' had failed. Defenders pointed to lower alcohol consumption and better health; critics pointed to crime, corruption, and disrespect for law. The debate ran on unresolved through 1924, with the drys still holding Congress and repeal advocates gaining ground.

pageData.title: Black Education and Politics: Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois
pageData.titleline: Black Education and Politics: Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois - The History Web
pageData.para1: When Reconstruction ended in 1877, the federal government stopped protecting the rights of formerly enslaved people in the South. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and violence stripped most Black Southerners of the vote, and Jim Crow laws imposed rigid segregation in schools, trains, and public places. In this harsh world, two Black leaders offered very different strategies for advancement. Booker T. Washington, born enslaved in Virginia in 1856, worked in salt furnaces and coal mines as a boy before making his way to Virginia's Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute in 1872, where he worked as a janitor to pay his expenses. In 1881 he was chosen to lead a new school for Black students at Tuskegee, Alabama, which he built from two small converted buildings into the Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute.
pageData.para2: Washington argued that Black Americans should first win economic security through vocational training, farming, and property ownership, trusting that prosperity would earn civil rights later. He summarized this approach at the Atlanta Exposition on September 18, 1895, telling a racially mixed audience, "In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress." White politicians and wealthy industrialists made him their preferred Black spokesman, and his autobiography Up from Slavery (1901) made him internationally famous. Critics called his position the Atlanta Compromise and warned that it accepted second-class citizenship.
pageData.para3: W.E.B. Du Bois came to the opposite conclusion. Born free in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, in 1868, he graduated from Fisk University in 1888 and in 1895 became the first Black person to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard University. In The Souls of Black Folk (1903), he charged that Washington's program asked Black people to surrender political power, civil rights, and higher education, and he argued for developing a "Talented Tenth" of college-trained Black leaders. In 1905 he helped organize the Niagara Movement for open protest, and in 1909 he cofounded the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), editing its magazine, The Crisis, from its founding in 1910.
pageData.para4: The Washington-Du Bois debate set the terms of Black public life for a generation. Tuskegee trained thousands of teachers and farmers and became the model for Black industrial education, while the NAACP fought lynching and segregation in the courts and the press. By the early 1920s Du Bois was also linking the struggle of Black Americans to peoples of African descent worldwide through the Pan-African Congresses. Although the two men disagreed bitterly, together they built the institutions, Black colleges and a national civil rights organization, that carried the fight for equality forward.

pageData.title: The Acadian Expulsion
pageData.titleline: The Acadian Expulsion - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Acadians were French-speaking farmers who settled the marshlands around the Bay of Fundy from 1604, building dikes to reclaim rich farmland from the tides. When mainland Nova Scotia passed to Britain by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, the Acadians found themselves a French Catholic majority under British Protestant rule. They asked to remain neutral in the empire's wars, refusing an unconditional oath of allegiance that might force them to fight France, and for decades British governors tolerated this 'neutrality'. By the 1750s, however, war with France was returning, and British officials came to see some fourteen thousand neutral Acadians as a threat at Britain's back.
pageData.para2: In the summer of 1755, after British and New England forces captured the French Fort Beauséjour, Governor Charles Lawrence and his council resolved to remove the Acadians entirely. The blow fell first at Grand-Pré: on 5 September 1755 the men and boys of the district were summoned to the village church, told their lands and livestock were forfeit, and held prisoner until ships arrived. Over the following months roughly seven thousand Acadians were herded aboard vessels while their farms and villages were burned; by the time the removals ended around 1764, some eleven thousand five hundred of eighteen thousand had been deported, and families were deliberately scattered.
pageData.para3: The exiles were dumped along the Atlantic seaboard from Massachusetts to Georgia, where colonial assemblies often refused them help, or shipped to Britain and later France. Hundreds died of smallpox and other shipboard diseases, and hundreds more drowned in 1758 when overcrowded transports such as the Duke William and the Violet sank in the Atlantic. Not all submitted: many Acadians escaped to the woods, to Quebec, or to Île Saint-Jean, and fighters like Joseph Broussard, called Beausoleil, waged guerrilla war along the Petitcodiac and St. John rivers against the deportation.
pageData.para4: New England 'Planters' were brought in to farm the emptied dykelands from 1760. When the surviving exiles were permitted to return from 1764, their best lands were gone, and they rebuilt on the margins of Nova Scotia and in what became New Brunswick, while others found their way to Louisiana, where they became the Cajuns. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's 1847 poem Evangeline fixed the tragedy in world memory. The Acadian nation the British meant to dissolve endured, and its descendants still call the deportation le Grand Dérangement, the Great Upheaval.

pageData.title: The Rebellions of 1837-1838 in Upper and Lower Canada
pageData.titleline: The Rebellions of 1837-1838 in Upper and Lower Canada - The History Web
pageData.para1: In the 1830s the two British colonies of Upper Canada (today's Ontario) and Lower Canada (today's Quebec) seethed with grievance. Real power lay with the lieutenant governors and small appointed oligarchies - the Family Compact in the upper province and the Château Clique in the lower - while elected assemblies could be ignored. In Lower Canada the conflict cut deeper still, because the English-speaking commercial minority governed a French-speaking majority, and reformers in the Parti patriote under Louis-Joseph Papineau had seen their Ninety-Two Resolutions of 1834 rejected outright. In Upper Canada the fiery journalist William Lyon Mackenzie denounced land speculation and privilege. When Britain answered reform demands with the hard-line Russell Resolutions of 1837, and an economic depression bit, armed revolt followed.
pageData.para2: Lower Canada rose first. After a vast open-air assembly at Saint-Charles in October 1837, Patriote militants clashed with British troops: they won at Saint-Denis on 23 November, were crushed at Saint-Charles two days later, and made their last stand at Saint-Eustache on 14 December, where troops killed some seventy defenders and burned the village. Papineau and other leaders fled to the United States. A second rising in 1838, led by the Frères chasseurs under Robert Nelson, who proclaimed a Canadian republic, was defeated at Odelltown and Lacolle. Reprisals were severe: twelve Patriotes were hanged in Montreal and fifty-eight more transported to the penal colonies of Australia.
pageData.para3: Upper Canada's rebellion was smaller and briefer. In December 1837 Mackenzie led a few hundred ill-armed farmers down Yonge Street toward Toronto, where loyalist militia scattered them near Montgomery's Tavern. Mackenzie escaped to Navy Island on the Niagara River and proclaimed a provisional government, and Canadian militia's destruction of the American supply steamer Caroline nearly dragged the United States into war. Through 1838 refugee 'Patriot' hunters launched border raids - at Short Hills, at Prescott's windmill, and near Windsor - all beaten back.
pageData.para4: Britain sent Lord Durham to investigate. His 1839 report famously called the quarrel 'two nations warring in the bosom of a single state', urged the union of the two colonies and the assimilation of French Canadians, but also recommended that the executive answer to the elected assembly. The Act of Union joined the Canadas in 1841, and by 1848-49 responsible government was won under LaFontaine and Baldwin, peacefully securing much of what the rebels had demanded. The failed rebellions thus became a hinge on the road to Canadian self-government and, ultimately, Confederation.

pageData.title: The Métis, Louis Riel and the Red River and North-West Resistances
pageData.titleline: The Métis, Louis Riel and the Red River and North-West Resistances - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Métis emerged from the fur trade as a distinct nation: children of First Nations mothers and French, Scottish, and English trader fathers, bound together by their own language, Michif, their Catholic and Protestant parishes, and the great semi-annual buffalo hunts of the Red River Settlement. When Canada arranged to buy the Hudson's Bay Company's vast territory of Rupert's Land in 1869, nobody consulted the roughly twelve thousand people of Red River. Canadian surveyors arrived marking out square lots across Métis river farms, and Ottawa's appointed governor was on his way. The Métis, led by the young, educated Louis Riel, decided their future would not be settled over their heads.
pageData.para2: In the autumn of 1869 the Métis National Committee blocked the governor's entry and seized Upper Fort Garry, and Riel formed a provisional government to negotiate terms of union. Its List of Rights produced the Manitoba Act of 1870, which brought Manitoba into Confederation with provincial status, language and school protections, and 1.4 million acres reserved for the children of Métis families. But the provisional government's court martial and execution of the belligerent Orangeman Thomas Scott made Riel a marked man in English Canada; when troops under Colonel Garnet Wolseley arrived in August 1870, Riel fled into exile. In the following years fraud and speculation stripped many Métis of their promised lands, and thousands moved west to the Saskatchewan country.
pageData.para3: There the pattern repeated: the buffalo collapsed, Ottawa ignored petitions over land and hunger, and in 1884 the Saskatchewan Métis sent for Riel. In March 1885 he proclaimed a second provisional government at Batoche, with the veteran hunt captain Gabriel Dumont as his general. The North-West Resistance that followed drew in some Cree as well: fighters of Wandering Spirit killed nine men at Frog Lake, while the great chiefs Poundmaker and Big Bear struggled to restrain their young men. Dumont beat back the Mounted Police at Duck Lake and held off General Middleton's column at Fish Creek, but Canadian soldiers carried the Métis lines at Batoche after four days of fighting in May 1885. Riel surrendered on 15 May.
pageData.para4: Riel was tried at Regina for high treason, and although the jury begged for mercy, Prime Minister John A. Macdonald let the sentence stand; he was hanged on 16 November 1885. Eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged at Battleford that November in Canada's largest mass execution, and Poundmaker and Big Bear went to prison. The resistance's defeat opened the prairies to the railway and settlement, and the Métis, their petitions ignored and their lands largely lost, were pushed to the margins of the society they had helped create. To French Canada Riel became a martyr; to the Métis, the founder of Manitoba and the symbol of a nation's survival.

pageData.title: Canada in the First World War: Vimy Ridge and Conscription
pageData.titleline: Canada in the First World War: Vimy Ridge and Conscription - The History Web
pageData.para1: When Britain declared war in August 1914, Canada, as a self-governing dominion of the Empire, was automatically at war, and Prime Minister Robert Borden threw the country in wholeheartedly. Within weeks a first contingent of over thirty thousand volunteers was sailing for England, the beginning of a Canadian Expeditionary Force that would enlist more than 620,000 men and women from a nation of eight million. The Canadians' blooding came at the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915, where they held the line through the first poison gas attacks of the western front at a cost of six thousand casualties, and then in the mud of the Somme in 1916.
pageData.para2: The Canadian Corps won its defining victory at Vimy Ridge in April 1917. For the first time all four Canadian divisions attacked together, behind meticulous preparation by commanders such as Arthur Currie: miles of tunnels, rehearsed infantry tactics, and a perfectly timed creeping artillery barrage. In four days, from 9 to 12 April, the Corps took the ridge that French attacks had failed to hold, at a cost of nearly 3,600 dead. Hill 70 and Passchendaele followed in 1917, and in 1918 the Corps spearheaded the Allied advance of Canada's Hundred Days from Amiens to Mons. By the armistice the Canadians were regarded as shock troops; some 61,000 had died and 172,000 been wounded.
pageData.para3: The war divided Canada at home. Volunteering slowed as casualty lists lengthened, and in 1917 Borden brought in the Military Service Act, imposing conscription. Quebec, where few French Canadians felt ties to either empire, rose in anger: Henri Bourassa campaigned against the law, and anti-conscription riots in Quebec City at Easter 1918 left four civilians dead. Borden's Union government won the bitter 'khaki election' of December 1917 with a franchise manipulated by the Wartime Elections Act, which gave the vote to women with soldiers in the family while stripping it from immigrants naturalized from enemy countries. Farmers, promised their sons would be exempt, saw the exemption cancelled after the vote.
pageData.para4: The war's aftermath carried Canada toward autonomy. Borden insisted on a distinct Canadian signature on the Treaty of Versailles and a separate seat in the new League of Nations; in 1922 Canada declined to rally automatically to Britain in the Chanak crisis, and in 1923 it signed the Halibut Treaty with the United States without a British countersignature, a first in imperial history. At home the country counted the cost in pensions, memorials, and a deepened French-English divide that the conscription struggle had carved into Canadian politics.

pageData.title: Zacatecas and the Colonial Silver Economy
pageData.titleline: Zacatecas and the Colonial Silver Economy - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1546, barely a generation after the fall of the Aztec Empire, Spanish prospectors in the arid hills north of Mexico City struck one of the richest silver deposits on Earth, and the city of Zacatecas rose from the mining camp almost overnight. Along with Guanajuato and San Luis Potosí it anchored the silver economy of New Spain, and by the late sixteenth century Zacatecas was among the largest cities in the Americas, a place of wealthy mine owners, grand churches, and refining mills built beside the shafts. The silver it pulled from the earth did not stay in Mexico: it flowed up the Camino Real to Mexico City and Veracruz, across the Atlantic in the treasure fleets, and across the Pacific in the Manila galleons, becoming the first truly global money.
pageData.para2: The mines ran on Indigenous labour. The Spanish first worked them with enslaved and tribute workers, then increasingly through the repartimiento, a rotating draft of village labourers, and wage workers drawn from communities uprooted by conquest and disease. Conditions underground were brutal: flooding shafts, mercury fumes from the patio refining process that used mercury to separate silver from ore, and death from accidents were routine. Yet the mining economy also created room for Indigenous and mixed-descent people to work, trade, and resist: the Chichimec peoples of the northern frontier fought the mining frontier in the long Chichimeca War of 1550-1590, forcing the crown to settle allied Tlaxcalan families in the region and to pay for peace with gifts and food.
pageData.para3: Silver shaped everything around it. A chain of garrison towns and haciendas grew along the Camino Real to supply the mines with food, mercury from Almadén, and cloth; mule trains linked Zacatecas to ports and fairs; and the crown taxed production through the quinto, the royal fifth, making mining revenue a pillar of Spanish imperial finance. The great bonanzas made individual fortunes, but the wealth was concentrated: most miners remained poor wage labourers, and the countryside around the mines was transformed into estates supplying the camps.
pageData.para4: Through the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Zacatecas silver helped pay for Spain's wars and bought the goods of Asia, tying the Americas, Europe, and China into one trading system. The city's wealth left a built legacy of aqueducts, convents, and one of the finest baroque cathedrals in Mexico. When the wars of independence disrupted the mines after 1810, the fragility of an economy built on a single metal was laid bare, but the pattern set in Zacatecas - booms financed by foreign capital, worked by local labour - would define Mexican mining for centuries.
