pageData.title: The Bourbon Reforms in New Spain
pageData.titleline: The Bourbon Reforms in New Spain - The History Web
pageData.para1: When the Bourbon dynasty took the Spanish throne in 1700, and especially after Charles III came to power in 1759, Spain set out to overhaul its American empire. New Spain, the viceroyalty stretching from Central America to the northern borderlands of today's United States, was the jewel of that empire, and the Bourbon kings wanted more of its wealth and tighter control over its government. The shock of the Seven Years' War, when Britain seized Havana in 1762, convinced Madrid that its colonies had to be defended and taxed far more effectively.
pageData.para2: The reforms touched everything. Charles III's inspector-general José de Gálvez spent 1765-1771 in New Spain reorganizing tax collection, establishing royal monopolies on tobacco, gunpowder, and playing cards, and raising revenue sharply. The old system of governing through officials who had bought their posts, many of them American-born creoles, was replaced by the intendancy system introduced in 1786: salaried provincial governors sent from Spain. The crown created a standing colonial army of regulars and militia, promoted mining with a new code and technical schools, and in 1804 even ordered the wealth of the colonial church funnelled to the royal treasury through the Consolidation decree.
pageData.para3: The most famous reform was the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767, when thousands of members of the order were deported from Spanish America and their missions, colleges, and estates seized. In New Spain's far north the crown filled the vacuum by reorganizing the frontier as the Commandancy General of the Interior Provinces in 1776, and Franciscans took over mission work, including the chain of missions founded in Alta California from 1769. Commerce was liberalized within the empire by the 1778 free trade regulations, and Veracruz boomed as silver exports climbed to record levels.
pageData.para4: The reforms worked too well for Spain's own good. Revenue from New Spain soared, but creole elites, shut out of high office by peninsular Spaniards and hit by new taxes, grew resentful; the expulsion of the Jesuits removed both schools and defenders of the crown; and the new militias trained the very men who would fight in the wars of independence. When Napoleon's invasion of Spain in 1808 decapitated the monarchy, the imperial ties reformed so tightly snapped within two years in a struggle that began at Dolores in 1810.

pageData.title: The War of Reform and Benito Juárez
pageData.titleline: The War of Reform and Benito Juárez - The History Web
pageData.para1: In the 1850s Mexico's exhausted politics split into two irreconcilable camps. Liberals, inspired by the generation that came of age after the disasters of the Texas revolt and the American war, blamed the country's weakness on the privileged corporations of colonial society: the army, with its own courts, and the Catholic Church, which held perhaps half of all productive property and its own legal jurisdiction. Conservatives defended church, army, and tradition as the only bonds holding Mexico together. When a liberal revolution in 1854, the Revolution of Ayutla, overthrew the dictator Santa Anna, the new generation led by Benito Juárez, a Zapotec lawyer from Oaxaca who had risen from poverty, set out to remake the country.
pageData.para2: The reform came in laws: the Ley Juárez of 1855 abolished the special courts of the military and clergy; the Ley Lerdo of 1856 ordered the sale of corporate lands, above all the church's rural estates; and the liberal Constitution of 1857 enshrined individual rights, secular authority, and federalism. The church excommunicated its defenders and conservatives rose in arms. In January 1858 the War of the Reform began, with two rival governments: the constitutional liberals under Juárez, who became president by constitutional succession, holding out at Veracruz, and the conservatives occupying Mexico City.
pageData.para3: The war devastated Mexico for three years. Juárez's government survived on Veracruz's customs revenue while its generals gradually mastered the battlefield, and the liberals answered conservative atrocities with radical decrees: in 1859 the Laws of Reform proclaimed from Veracruz nationalized all church property without compensation, suppressed the male religious orders, established civil marriage and civil registries, and separated church and state. On 22 December 1860 the liberal army won the decisive battle of Calpulalpan, and on New Year's Day 1861 Juárez entered Mexico City in triumph.
pageData.para4: Victory left Mexico ruined and divided, and its debts gave Europe a pretext to intervene: within a year French troops landed, beginning the adventure of Maximilian's empire. But the Reform endured. Juárez's laws broke the economic power of the colonial church, created a class of property holders from its former estates, and made the liberal Constitution the standard around which Mexico rallied through the French intervention and beyond. For Mexicans, Juárez, the Indigenous president who never learned Spanish until his teens, became the embodiment of the nation's republican dignity: 'among individuals as among nations, respect for the rights of others is peace.'

pageData.title: The French Intervention and the Second Mexican Empire
pageData.titleline: The French Intervention and the Second Mexican Empire - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1861 President Benito Juárez, inheriting a treasury emptied by the War of the Reform, suspended payments on Mexico's foreign debts. Britain, Spain, and France signed the Convention of London and sent fleets to Veracruz to collect. Britain and Spain soon saw that Napoleon III of France had larger ambitions - he dreamed of a Catholic Latin empire in America and a canal across the isthmus - and withdrew in 1862. France pressed on alone. On 5 May 1862 the French army marching on Mexico City was beaten at Puebla by Mexican forces under Ignacio Zaragoza, a victory still celebrated as Cinco de Mayo, but Napoleon poured in reinforcements, and in June 1863 French troops entered the capital.
pageData.para2: Napoleon's design needed a throne, and he offered it to the Habsburg archduke Ferdinand Maximilian, who accepted after a staged plebiscite and landed at Veracruz in 1864 with his wife Carlota. The Second Mexican Empire that followed was a strange mixture: Maximilian was a sincere liberal who kept the Reform's land sales, confirmed freedom of religion, and won over some old liberals, while conservatives who had invited him despaired at his moderation. He built a court at Chapultepec Castle, drove the great boulevard now called Reforma, and ruled with real ambition but shrinking means as French subsidies dried up.
pageData.para3: Outside the capital the empire never rested. Juárez refused to recognize the invaders and led a government on the run, carrying the republic's archives north to the city that still bears his name, Ciudad Juárez, while republican armies under generals like Porfirio Díaz and Mariano Escobedo bled the occupation in guerrilla war. The empire answered with terror: the 'Black Decree' of October 1865 ordered captured republicans shot as bandits. From 1865 the United States, its own civil war over, massed troops on the Rio Grande and armed Juárez, and Napoleon III, facing Prussia at home, ordered his legions out; the last French troops sailed in early 1867.
pageData.para4: Maximilian refused to abandon the throne and was besieged at Querétaro with his remaining Mexican imperialists. Captured in May 1867, he was tried by court martial and shot on the Cerro de las Campanas on 19 June 1867 beside his generals Miramón and Mejía. Juárez entered Mexico City in July and was re-elected president. The intervention left Mexico's republican institutions intact and forged the nationalism of a generation, while in Europe Manet's great painting of the execution fixed the empire's fall as a warning against imperial adventures.

pageData.title: The Porfiriato: Railways, Growth and Inequality
pageData.titleline: The Porfiriato: Railways, Growth and Inequality - The History Web
pageData.para1: Porfirio Díaz, a Mixtec-descended general and hero of the war against the French, seized the Mexican presidency in 1876 and, except for one interlude from 1880 to 1884, ruled Mexico until 1911 - an era Mexicans call the Porfiriato. He promised 'order and progress', and delivered both on ruthless terms: bandits were hunted down by the rural police, rebellious generals were bought or shot, elections were staged, and regional bosses who accepted the system prospered while those who resisted disappeared. Under the slogan 'little politics and much administration', Díaz gave Mexico its first durable peace since independence, at the price of its liberty.
pageData.para2: Peace, plus generous concessions, unleashed foreign capital. American and British investors built the railways that became the regime's emblem: the Mexican Central from the capital to El Paso in 1884, the Mexican National to Laredo, and the Veracruz line with its spectacular bridges over the barrancas, painted by José María Velasco. By 1910 Mexico had some 20,000 kilometres of track where it had had 700. Mines reopened with foreign technology, oil fields rose around Tampico, and exports soared; Díaz's finance minister José Yves Limantour balanced the budget and put Mexico on the gold standard.
pageData.para3: The statistics hid a social catastrophe. Survey laws let land companies declare village commons 'vacant', and by 1910 some ninety percent of rural families in the central plateau had lost their land; huge haciendas swallowed indigenous communities, and on the henequen plantations of Yucatán and the tobacco fields of the Valle Nacional, Yaqui and Maya deportees worked in conditions close to slavery. Real wages fell through the era even as the price of corn rose, and workers who protested met bullets: the strikes at the Cananea copper mine in 1906 and the Río Blanco textile mill in 1907 were broken by gunfire.
pageData.para4: Díaz's circle of technocrat advisers, the científicos, believed Mexico was being made modern by science and capital. Instead, the regime created the grievances that exploded in 1910: a dispossessed countryside, muzzled workers, excluded middle classes, and a dictator who had ruled for a generation. When Díaz told the American journalist James Creelman in 1908 that Mexico was ready for democracy, the opposition took him at his word, and the Porfiriato collapsed into the Mexican Revolution. Its railways and monuments remained; so did the question of who owned Mexico's land.

pageData.title: The Mexican Revolution and the Constitution of 1917
pageData.titleline: The Mexican Revolution and the Constitution of 1917 - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Mexican Revolution began in 1910 when Francisco Madero, a wealthy landowner's son, challenged the aged dictator Porfirio Díaz in the presidential election, was jailed, and called the nation to arms for 20 November under the Plan de San Luis Potosí. Uprisings by farmers under Pascual Orozco in Chihuahua and Emiliano Zapata in Morelos toppled Díaz in May 1911. But Madero's revolution was political, while his followers wanted land: Zapata rose again under the Plan de Ayala demanding that the villages' stolen fields be returned, and in February 1913 Madero was overthrown and murdered in a coup by the general Victoriano Huerta, backed by the conservative establishment.
pageData.para2: Huerta's dictatorship united Mexico against him. Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, raised the Constitutionalist Army; Alvaro Obregón, a farmer turned brilliant general, campaigned down the Pacific coast; Pancho Villa's Division of the North drove south from Chihuahua; and Zapata's agrarian rebels held the south. Huerta fell in July 1914, but the victors then turned on one another: at the Convention of Aguascalientes the alliances shattered, and in 1915 Obregón crushed Villa in the great battles of Celaya, reducing the revolution's war of movement to a grinding regional struggle.
pageData.para3: Out of the bloodshed came a remarkable constitution. Carranza, needing to outbid the radicals, summoned a congress at Querétaro, and the Constitution of 1917 that emerged was the most radical charter of its age: Article 27 declared the nation's ownership of land and subsoil, opening the way to agrarian reform and control of oil; Article 123 gave workers the eight-hour day, the right to organize and strike; Article 3 established free, secular education; and the church was stripped of legal personality and property. Zapata was assassinated by treachery in 1919 and Villa retired in 1920 after Obregón and his allies overthrew Carranza.
pageData.para4: By 1920 a decade of fighting, famine, and disease had devastated Mexico. Reconstruction began under Obregón, president from December 1920, who started land distribution, a vast rural school program under José Vasconcelos, and the muralist movement; his successor Plutarco Elías Calles took office on 1 December 1924. The revolution's settlement - land reform, labour rights, secular nationalism, and the constitutional state - defined Mexico for the twentieth century. The United States' own forays, the 1914 occupation of Veracruz and the 1916 Punitive Expedition chasing Villa into Chihuahua, showed how closely the revolution and its northern neighbour remained entangled.

pageData.title: Mexico's Cultural Renaissance and Early Muralism, 1920-1924
pageData.titleline: Mexico's Cultural Renaissance and Early Muralism, 1920-1924 - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Mexico that emerged from a decade of revolution in 1920 was exhausted, but it was also seized by a creative energy that astonished the world. President Alvaro Obregón and his minister of education José Vasconcelos believed the revolution had to remake not only property and politics but the Mexican soul. Vasconcelos's Secretariat of Public Education, created in 1921, sent teachers, books, and 'cultural missions' into the countryside, founded hundreds of rural schools, printed cheap editions of the classics, and preached a nationalism that exalted Mexico's Indigenous heritage as the source of its identity - a movement called indigenismo.
pageData.para2: The most visible fruit was muralism. Vasconcelos offered the walls of public buildings to young painters, commissioning them to paint the nation's history for a people who could not all read. Diego Rivera, home from Europe in 1921, painted his first mural, Creation, in the Simón Bolívar Amphitheatre of the old San Ildefonso college in 1922, while José Clemente Orozco began his fierce early frescoes in the same building in 1923, and David Alfaro Siqueiros organized the artists' syndicate and its manifesto demanding a public, monumental, and social art. In 1923-24 Rivera started his vast cycle in the courtyards of the new Ministry of Education, painting festivals, labour, and the revolutionary epic.
pageData.para3: The renaissance ran far wider than the murals. Anthropologists such as Manuel Gamio were recovering Teotihuacan and revaluing Indigenous Mexico; composers like Carlos Chávez built a national music on Indigenous themes; the open-air art schools took painting to the barrios; and printmakers revived the popular broadside tradition of José Guadalupe Posada, whose images the artists' newspaper El Machete carried to a mass public. Adolfo Best Maugard's drawing method, based on the motifs of pre-Hispanic art, was taught in the schools as the grammar of a national style.
pageData.para4: By the end of 1924, when Plutarco Elías Calles succeeded Obregón, the cultural program was firmly established. Its artists and teachers placed Indigenous history and popular culture at the centre of a new national story, even as Indigenous peoples remained more often represented than heard.

pageData.title: The Jamaican Maroons and Resistance to Slavery
pageData.titleline: The Jamaican Maroons and Resistance to Slavery - The History Web
pageData.para1: Across the slaveholding Americas, men and women who fled the plantations built free communities in wild country, and nowhere did they succeed so completely as in Jamaica. The island's Maroons began with the Africans freed or abandoned when Britain seized Jamaica from Spain in 1655; reinforced by generations of runaways from the sugar estates, they formed two nations: the Leeward Maroons in the cockpit country of Trelawney and the Windward Maroons in the Blue Mountains. From these near-impenetrable refuges, ruled by their own chiefs and councils, they raided plantations, drew off more fugitives, and defeated every army sent against them for eighty years.
pageData.para2: Maroon strength rested on mastery of the land and of guerrilla war. They farmed hidden provision grounds, communicated across the mountains with the abeng horn, and ambushed British columns in country where redcoats could not form a line. Under leaders like the Windward chief Nanny, the Maroons' most famous commander, and the Leeward chief Cudjoe, the Maroons fought the First Maroon War to exhaustion on both sides. In 1739 Cudjoe forced Britain to a treaty recognizing the Maroons' freedom and their lands, in return for an end to raids and a promise to return future runaways; Nanny's people signed the following year.
pageData.para3: The treaties held for half a century, then broke in blood. In 1795 a dispute over the flogging of two Trelawney Maroons exploded into the Second Maroon War, and five hundred Trelawney Maroons tied down thousands of British troops for five months. Beaten by imported bloodhounds and tricked by a negotiated surrender, nearly six hundred Trelawney Maroons were deported first to Nova Scotia and then, in 1800, to Sierra Leone - a betrayal that emptied the most defiant Maroon nation. The Windward Maroons of Moore Town, Charles Town, and Scott's Hall remained, and their lands survive today.
pageData.para4: The Maroons proved that enslaved Africans could defeat the British Empire and force it to recognize their freedom, and their example shadowed every Jamaican slaveholder thereafter. Their treaties of 1739-40 were among the first recognitions of a free Black polity in the British Atlantic, and the maroon ideal - freedom won and defended in the mountains - inspired later generations of Jamaican resistance, from the Baptist War of 1831-32 to Morant Bay in 1865.

pageData.title: Emancipation and Apprenticeship in the British Caribbean
pageData.titleline: Emancipation and Apprenticeship in the British Caribbean - The History Web
pageData.para1: On 1 August 1834 the Slavery Abolition Act took effect across most British colonies, giving legal freedom to more than eight hundred thousand people in the Caribbean, South Africa, and Canada, although compulsory apprenticeship continued for many. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 was the fruit of half a century of abolitionist campaigning and, just as much, of resistance by the enslaved themselves, whose great revolts - Barbados in 1816, Demerara in 1823, and above all Jamaica's Baptist War of 1831-32, in which sixty thousand enslaved people rose - convinced Britain that slavery could no longer be sustained. Parliament voted the enormous sum of twenty million pounds in compensation, all of it to the slaveholders; the people they had enslaved received nothing but freedom by instalments.
pageData.para2: For the Act granted freedom in name first. All children under six were freed outright, but everyone else was bound as an 'apprentice', compelled to work forty-five unpaid hours a week for their former masters - field hands for six years, domestic workers for four - in exchange for food, housing, and the promise of full liberty. The planters used the courts and the treadmill to punish apprentices, and the scheme's injustice was so plain that a new abolitionist campaign, with the apprentices' own strikes and refusals behind it, forced the colonial assemblies to end the system early. On 1 August 1838 full freedom came, two years ahead of schedule, celebrated in chapels and streets from Antigua to Demerara.
pageData.para3: Freedom's first test was land. The planters meant to keep the freed people working on the estates by holding the land and setting rents and wages; the freed people meant to farm their own. In Jamaica and Demerara they bought bankrupt estates and squatted on Crown lands, raising a free peasantry of provision farmers - in Jamaica the 'free villages' founded with Baptist missionaries, like Sturge Town and Sligoville, became symbols of the new order. Planters answered by importing labour: from 1838 hundreds of thousands of indentured workers came from India, and smaller numbers from China, Madeira, and Africa, beginning a transformation of the region's peoples as profound as emancipation itself.
pageData.para4: The apprenticeship experiment and its collapse defined British Caribbean freedom. The freed people had won, through their own resistance, both emancipation and its acceleration, and they built independent communities in the face of planter power; but the colonial state left them landless enough to keep the sugar estates alive, and poverty and colour bars would fuel the struggles that erupted at Morant Bay in 1865 and beyond. First of August, Emancipation Day, remains the great commemoration of the region.

pageData.title: The Morant Bay Rebellion
pageData.titleline: The Morant Bay Rebellion - The History Web
pageData.para1: In October 1865 the parish of St. Thomas-in-the-East in Jamaica rose in the last great rebellion of the island's nineteenth century. A generation after emancipation, Jamaica's Black majority remained landless and voteless: wages on the sugar estates had collapsed, drought and the American Civil War had raised prices, a poll tax kept nearly all Black men off the electoral roll, and the courts answered their grievances with contempt. A Native Baptist deacon and landowner, Paul Bogle, had led his neighbours' protests to the colonial government; when Governor Edward Eyre ignored their petition, tension in the parish mounted toward explosion.
pageData.para2: The spark was a court case. On 7 October 1865 a man was arrested at the Morant Bay courthouse for interrupting the trial of a squatter; when Bogle's men rescued another prisoner days later, warrants were issued, and on 11 October several hundred protesters marched on the courthouse. The volunteer militia fired into the crowd, killing seven, and the crowd stormed and burned the building, killing the custos, the parish's chief magistrate, and seventeen others. For days the rising spread through the parish's estates, and two planters were killed. Bogle's ally, the mixed-race assemblyman and Baptist advocate George William Gordon, was in Kingston when it began.
pageData.para3: The government's vengeance vastly exceeded the rising. Eyre declared martial law, and for a month soldiers and Maroon irregulars swept St. Thomas-in-the-East: by official count 439 people were killed, more than six hundred flogged, and a thousand houses burned. Gordon was seized in Kingston, dragged into the martial-law zone, convicted by a hasty court martial, and hanged on 23 October; Bogle was hanged the next day. The brutality split Britain itself: a Jamaica Committee under John Stuart Mill demanded Eyre's prosecution while Charles Dickens and Thomas Carlyle defended him, and though Eyre was recalled and never tried, Jamaica's two-century-old assembly was abolished and the island made a Crown Colony.
pageData.para4: Morant Bay exposed the unfinished business of emancipation: freedom without land, vote, or justice. Crown Colony rule brought some reforms but no democracy, and the struggle Bogle and Gordon died for - land, justice, and political voice - ran on into the twentieth century.

pageData.title: Puerto Rico from Spanish to US Rule, 1898-1924
pageData.titleline: Puerto Rico from Spanish to US Rule, 1898-1924 - The History Web
pageData.para1: In November 1897 Spain, fighting for its last Caribbean colonies, granted Puerto Rico an Autonomic Charter, and the island's first autonomous government under Luis Muñoz Rivera had barely taken office when the Spanish-American War made it a prize of war. On 25 July 1898 United States troops landed at Guánica and swept across the island in a three-week campaign, welcomed by many Puerto Ricans who hoped for expansion of the new autonomy. Instead, by the Treaty of Paris that December, Spain ceded Puerto Rico to the United States, and the island passed under military government without a single Puerto Rican signature on the treaty that decided its fate.
pageData.para2: American rule began with economic transformation and political limbo. The Foraker Act of 1900 replaced the military regime with a civil government - a governor and supreme court appointed in Washington, an elected lower house - and the Supreme Court's Insular Cases declared Puerto Rico an 'unincorporated territory' that 'belonged to but was not part of' the United States, with no promise of statehood or independence. Hurricane San Ciriaco in 1899 devastated the coffee economy, and American sugar corporations moved into the vacuum: by the 1920s four companies dominated a sugar industry that absorbed farmland and turned independent farmers into seasonal wage workers.
pageData.para3: Puerto Ricans organized through every channel open to them. The Unionist party pressed for self-government; the Socialist party of Santiago Iglesias grew with the cane workers' strikes; the Nationalist movement gathered the independence tradition that ran back to the Grito de Lares of 1868. In 1917 the Jones Act answered part of the demand: Puerto Ricans became United States citizens - weeks before the nation entered the First World War, in which some eighteen thousand islanders served - and won an elected senate and a bill of rights, though the governor still ruled from Washington's appointment.
pageData.para4: By 1924 the island lived under the settlement of 1917: American citizenship without a vote for president, an economy recast around sugar and migration, and a politics organized around the status question - statehood, autonomy, or independence - that the events of 1898 had created. The autonomists' brief triumph of 1897 remained the measure of what had been lost and the model for what many still sought.

pageData.title: The Comanche and the Horse-Based Plains Economy
pageData.titleline: The Comanche and the Horse-Based Plains Economy - The History Web
pageData.para1: In the early eighteenth century, the Comanche were one small Shoshonean people of the Wyoming mountains. Within a few generations they had transformed themselves into the dominant power of the southern Great Plains. The key was the horse. Moving south onto the plains, Comanche bands adopted a fully mounted way of life, becoming such skilled riders and breeders that observers called them the finest light cavalry in the world. By about 1750 they had driven the Apache from the southern plains and ruled a vast territory, Comancheria, stretching across what are now Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, New Mexico and Colorado.
pageData.para2: Comanche society was built on the buffalo and the raid. Vast herds provided food, tipi covers, clothing and rawhide, while organized raiding into Spanish Texas and, especially, northern Mexico brought horses, mules, captives and guns. Women processed the hides and dried meat that underpinned the economy; men won status through war honors and generosity. Several autonomous bands shared a language and culture but no central government, with peace chiefs and war chiefs leading by reputation. Trading fairs, notably at Taos, turned Comancheria into the commercial hub of the Southwest, exchanging buffalo products, horses and captives for guns, cloth, maize and metalware.
pageData.para3: For a century Comanche power bent empires around it. Spanish officials, unable to defeat them, sued for peace in 1786, and for decades New Mexico's frontier settlements paid a kind of tribute in gifts and trade to keep the peace. Comanche and allied Kiowa raiders ranged deep into Mexico, contributing to the collapse of Spanish authority on its northern frontier and, later, challenging the young Mexican republic and the expanding United States. Captives taken on raids were often adopted into the bands, a practice that kept Comanche numbers up even as epidemics struck.
pageData.para4: Comanche supremacy rested on fragile foundations. After mid-century, American hunters slaughtered the buffalo herds on an industrial scale, cholera and smallpox cut the population, and US military campaigns pressed in from every side. The last free bands, led by the Kwahadi chief Quanah Parker, surrendered at Fort Sill in 1875 and settled on a reservation in Oklahoma. Yet the Comanche Nation endured: today it is a sovereign nation that honors this history of adaptation, horsemanship and power, a reminder that for over a century the southern plains were not a colonial frontier but an Indigenous empire.

pageData.title: Jamestown and the Virginia Company
pageData.titleline: Jamestown and the Virginia Company - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1606 King James I chartered the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock enterprise of investors hoping for gold, a passage to Asia, and profit from North America. The next year three ships, the Susan Constant, Godspeed and Discovery, carried about 104 men and boys up a river they named for their king, where they built a triangular timber fort on a marshy peninsula: Jamestown, the first permanent English settlement in what became the United States. The site was defensible but unhealthy, and the gentlemen-heavy company was ill-prepared to feed itself.
pageData.para2: The colony nearly died. Disease, brackish water and hunger killed most of the first settlers within a year, and the 'starving time' winter of 1609-1610 reduced several hundred colonists to sixty, with some resorting to cannibalism. Survival depended on the soldiers' discipline enforced by leaders like John Smith, on shiploads of new recruits, and on the food of the surrounding Powhatan people, who traded, and sometimes withheld, the corn that kept the colony alive. The Virginia Company poured in money and settlers and got almost nothing back.
pageData.para3: Virginia's salvation was a weed. John Rolfe's experiments with West Indian tobacco produced a smooth, marketable leaf, and by the later 1610s tobacco exports were booming, turning the struggling outpost into a boomtown of plantations strung along the river. Rolfe's marriage to Pocahontas in 1614 sealed a temporary peace with Powhatan. To attract settlers the company granted private land through the headright system and, in 1619, summoned an elected House of Burgesses, the first representative assembly in English America. That same year a ship landed the first recorded Africans in the colony, 'twenty and odd' captives whose status was then still undefined.
pageData.para4: In 1622 Powhatan's successor Opechancanough struck the colony in a coordinated assault that killed roughly a third of its people. The crown used the disaster, and the company's mounting failures, to revoke the charter in 1624, making Virginia a royal colony. Jamestown remained its capital until 1699, when the seat of government moved to Williamsburg, and the old town dwindled into farmland and pasture. Much of the site survived on land, and antiquarian and archaeological work there has recovered the story of England's precarious American beginning.

pageData.title: Plymouth, the Wampanoag and the Mayflower Colony
pageData.titleline: Plymouth, the Wampanoag and the Mayflower Colony - The History Web
pageData.para1: In September 1620 the merchant ship Mayflower left England carrying 102 passengers. About a third were Separatists, religious dissenters who had broken with the Church of England and spent a decade in exile in the Dutch city of Leiden; the rest were 'Strangers,' workers, servants and adventurers sent by the voyage's investors. Blown north of their Hudson River destination, they anchored off Cape Cod. Because their patent did not cover this land, the leading men signed the Mayflower Compact aboard ship, pledging to form a 'civil body politic' bound by majority-agreed laws, a landmark of self-government, before anyone went ashore.
pageData.para2: The colonists settled at an abandoned Patuxet village they named Plymouth in December 1620, and the first winter killed half of them. They survived with help that was anything but accidental. Tisquantum, called Squanto, a Patuxet man who had been kidnapped to Europe and found his way home to an emptied land, taught the newcomers to plant corn with fish and navigate local diplomacy. In 1621 the settlers and the neighboring Wampanoag confederacy, led by the sachem Ousamequin (Massasoit), agreed a mutual-defense pact, and that autumn the two communities shared a harvest feast remembered as the first Thanksgiving.
pageData.para3: The Wampanoag had reasons of their own for the alliance. Epidemics brought by earlier European ships had killed as many as two-thirds of the coastal peoples between 1616 and 1619, leaving Massasoit's confederacy vulnerable to its Narragansett rivals. The alliance held for fifty years, but the peace depended on Massasoit's personal diplomacy as English numbers swelled from one town to many, steadily swallowing Native land, hunting grounds and authority.
pageData.para4: Plymouth Colony itself remained small, pious and self-governing, electing its governors and General Court, until it was absorbed into Massachusetts in 1691. Its larger legacy lies in the patterns it set: a covenant community bound by compact, a holiday built on a real but fragile moment of coexistence, and a warning. When Massasoit's son Metacom, called King Philip, watched the land and power of his people slip away, the unequal partnership collapsed into the terrible war of 1675 that forever changed New England.

pageData.title: Massachusetts Bay and Puritan New England
pageData.titleline: Massachusetts Bay and Puritan New England - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1630, a fleet of eleven ships carried about a thousand English Puritans across the Atlantic, the vanguard of a 'Great Migration' that would bring some 20,000 settlers to New England in a decade. Puritans were reformers who believed the Church of England had kept too much of Rome, and under pressure at home they organized the Massachusetts Bay Company, won a royal charter, and, uniquely, carried the charter itself to America, making their colony a largely self-governing commonwealth. Governor John Winthrop preached that their settlement should be 'as a city upon a hill,' a model of a godly society for the world to watch.
pageData.para2: Massachusetts Bay was planted as a chain of farming towns, each gathered around its meetinghouse, congregation and common fields. Land was distributed to town proprietors, men were expected to work farms and serve the community, and town meetings managed local affairs with remarkable directness. The colony's leaders built institutions for their vision: Harvard College was founded in 1636 to train ministers, and in 1647 Massachusetts passed the first general public-education law in English America, requiring towns to support schools so that children could read Scripture.
pageData.para3: This was also a society of strict boundaries. Voting and office belonged to male church members, and dissent could be dangerous: Roger Williams was banished for challenging the union of church and state and founded Providence in 1636, while Anne Hutchinson's theological challenge to the clergy ended in her exile in 1638. Ministers and magistrates policed doctrine, and the colony's courts enforced religious conformity as a matter of public order.
pageData.para4: Puritan confidence also collided with the land's first peoples. English settlement spread into Pequot, Massachusetts and Wampanoag country under pressure of epidemics and land sales, and in 1675-1676 King Philip's War devastated both Native nations and colonial towns. The colony lost its original charter in 1684 and became a royal province in 1691, absorbing Plymouth. Yet the town meeting, the schoolhouse, and the restless habit of building 'a city upon a hill' remained lasting bequests of the Puritan experiment.
pageData.source3label: Library of Congress: America as a Religious Refuge

pageData.title: New Netherland and the Dutch Atlantic
pageData.titleline: New Netherland and the Dutch Atlantic - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1609 Henry Hudson, an English captain sailing for the Dutch East India Company, explored the river that now bears his name and reported a land rich in furs. Dutch traders followed, and in 1624 the new Dutch West India Company planted permanent settlers, purchasing Manhattan Island from its Indigenous inhabitants in 1626 for goods famously valued at sixty guilders. The colony of New Netherland was never a farmer's refuge but a business venture: its purpose was profit, above all the beaver pelts that poured down the Hudson to Fort Orange, near today's Albany, one of the busiest fur markets in the Atlantic world.
pageData.para2: New Amsterdam, the little capital at Manhattan's tip, was a company town with a windmill, a fort and a waterfront of warehouses, and soon one of the most cosmopolitan places on earth. In 1643 a visiting Jesuit claimed to hear eighteen languages spoken there. Walloons, Germans, Scandinavians, Jews expelled from Brazil, free and enslaved Africans, and English Puritans all settled under Dutch rule. The colony's pragmatic tolerance was commercial as much as idealistic, but it gave New Netherland a plural character long before toleration was fashionable.
pageData.para3: The company's rule was often harsh and inept. Director-General Willem Kieft's reckless war against neighboring Native peoples in the 1640s devastated the colony and its fur trade; his successor, the one-legged Peter Stuyvesant, governed firmly, took the Swedish colony of New Sweden on the Delaware in 1655, and built New Amsterdam into an orderly port, though colonists chafed at having no elected assembly. Meanwhile the 'patroonship' system, vast manorial estates granted to wealthy investors, struggled to attract the farmers the colony needed.
pageData.para4: New Netherland fell without a shot. In August 1664 four English frigates appeared in the harbor, and Stuyvesant, unsupported by his company and facing citizens unwilling to fight, surrendered. The English renamed the province New York, and though the Dutch briefly retook it in 1673, the colony was gone by 1674. Its legacies endured: New York's commercial energy, ethnic diversity, legal customs and place names, from Harlem to Brooklyn, are the inheritance of the Dutch Atlantic's four decades on the Hudson.

pageData.source3label: National Park Service: New Netherland, the Dutch Commercial Colony

pageData.title: Pennsylvania and the Quaker Experiment
pageData.titleline: Pennsylvania and the Quaker Experiment - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1681 King Charles II granted William Penn an enormous tract of land west of the Delaware River, settling a crown debt to Penn's father and giving England's most persecuted sect a refuge. Penn was a Quaker, a member of the Society of Friends, whose belief in the 'Inner Light' in every person, refusal to swear oaths or remove their hats, and rejection of a paid clergy had landed thousands in English jails. His 'Holy Experiment' in Pennsylvania reversed the rules of the age: freedom of conscience for all monotheists, an elected assembly with real power, no established church, and no militia.
pageData.para2: Penn also treated the land's first peoples differently. Convinced that Indigenous nations held a just claim to their country, his government purchased land through treaties rather than seizing it, and under his lifetime Pennsylvania knew an almost unique peace with its Lenape and Susquehannock neighbors. The 1682 treaty at Shackamaxon became legendary as a model of fair dealing. That peace was real, but it rested on Penn's personal honor; after his death, his heirs' 'Walking Purchase' fraud of 1737 and the pressure of settlement poisoned what he had built.
pageData.para3: The colony grew with astonishing speed. Philadelphia, Penn's 'city of brotherly love,' laid out in a rational grid with public squares, became British America's largest city by the 1770s, a port funneling wheat, flour and lumber to the Atlantic world. Waves of immigrants, Welsh Quakers, German Mennonites and Pietists, Scots-Irish Presbyterians, were drawn by cheap land, religious freedom and peace. Prosperous farms in the limestone valleys made Pennsylvania the breadbasket of the colonies.
pageData.para4: Pennsylvania's experiment proved that a colony could thrive without coercion of conscience. Its Frame of Government, repeatedly revised at settlers' demand, pushed power toward an elected single-house assembly that became one of the most democratic bodies in the colonial world. Quaker influence also produced early testimony against slavery and war. Philadelphia's wealth, printers and civic institutions would later make it the natural capital of the American Revolution, a long harvest of the seeds Penn planted in 1682.
pageData.source3label: Library of Congress: Commerce in Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia

pageData.title: The Carolina Colonies and the Rice Economy
pageData.titleline: The Carolina Colonies and the Rice Economy - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1663 Charles II granted a vast coastal territory between Virginia and Spanish Florida to eight Lords Proprietors who had helped restore him to the throne. They named it Carolina and envisioned a hierarchical society under their elaborate, never-fully-imposed Fundamental Constitutions. Reality took a different course. Settlers from crowded Barbados arrived with enslaved Africans and a plantation model, while Virginians spread into the northern sounds. Charles Town, founded in 1670 on the harbor where two rivers meet, grew into the richest city in the southern colonies.
pageData.para2: Early Carolinians traded deerskins and naval stores with the region's Native nations and raised cattle in open pinewoods. Then, in the 1690s, planters proved that rice would thrive in the tidal swamps of the Lowcountry. Rice made Carolina a fortune, but it was a fortune built on African knowledge and African backs. The crop's engineering, clearing swamps, building banks, gates and trunks to manage tidal flooding, and its arduous processing, depended on the skills of enslaved people from West Africa's own rice coast, who were imported in huge numbers. By 1708 enslaved Africans were a majority of South Carolina's population.
pageData.para3: The plantation regime was maintained by force and resisted in kind. The 1739 Stono Rebellion, the colony's largest slave uprising, prompted the harsh Negro Act of 1740, which tightened every control on Black life. Yet in the isolation of swamp and sea island, enslaved people built the durable Gullah-Geechee culture, preserving African language, foodways and crafts. South Carolina split administratively from poorer, small-farm North Carolina in 1712, and both became royal colonies in 1729 after the proprietors' misrule and the Yamasee War had nearly broken them.
pageData.para4: Rice, indigo and the Atlantic trade made South Carolina's planters the wealthiest men in mainland British America, a gentry of townhouses, libraries and racehorses floating on enslaved labor. That wealth gave South Carolina outsized influence in the coming Revolution, and a fierce determination to defend the slavery that produced it, a contradiction written into American history from the very start.
pageData.source2label: National Park Service: Life and Labor at a Rice Plantation

pageData.title: Colonial Georgia and the Southern Frontier
pageData.titleline: Colonial Georgia and the Southern Frontier - The History Web
pageData.para1: Georgia, chartered in 1732, was the last of the thirteen colonies, founded with an unusual blend of philanthropy, idealism and strategy. Its moving spirit was James Edward Oglethorpe, a member of Parliament whose work on prison reform had exposed the misery of debtors' jails. The Georgia Trustees proposed a colony where the 'worthy poor' could farm small plots with dignity: land grants capped in size, rum banned, and slavery prohibited, partly on principle and partly so that small farmers, not planters, would man the frontier. For South Carolina, Georgia was also a buffer against Spanish Florida and its Native and French allies.
pageData.para2: Oglethorpe led the first settlers to Savannah in 1733, laying out the town's famous grid of wards and squares. He cultivated peace with the Yamacraw chief Tomochichi, who ceded the site and traveled to England, and negotiated with the powerful Creek confederacy. But Georgia's real test was war: when conflict with Spain came in 1739, Oglethorpe's invasion of Florida failed, and in 1742 a Spanish counterattack was bloodily repulsed at the Battle of Bloody Marsh on St. Simons Island, securing the colony's survival.
pageData.para3: The trustees' utopia eroded under pressure. Colonists resented the limits on landholding and complained they could not compete with slave-worked Carolina rice plantations. One by one the bans fell, on rum in 1742, on slavery in 1751, and with slavery came the plantation economy the founders had meant to prevent. In 1752 the trustees, disappointed and broke, surrendered their charter a year early, and Georgia became a royal colony.
pageData.para4: Royal Georgia boomed. Rice and indigo plantations spread along the coast, worked by enslaved Africans, while small farmers pushed into the Creek backcountry. Savannah grew into a busy Atlantic port. By the 1760s Georgia was British America's youngest and fastest-growing colony, its founders' experiment in a slave-free yeoman republic all but forgotten beneath the plantations of the southern frontier.

pageData.title: Maryland and the Chesapeake Tobacco Economy
pageData.titleline: Maryland and the Chesapeake Tobacco Economy - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1632 Charles I granted Cecil Calvert, the second Lord Baltimore, a colony north of the Potomac named for Queen Henrietta Maria. The Calverts were Catholic, and Maryland was conceived both as a profitable proprietary estate and as a haven where English Catholics could worship in peace. The first settlers landed in 1634, bought a village site from the Yaocomico people, who chose to relocate, and founded St. Mary's City. Because Catholics remained a minority in their own colony, the Calverts made tolerance policy: Maryland's 1649 Act Concerning Religion, among the first laws of its kind in the English world, guaranteed freedom of worship to all Trinitarian Christians.
pageData.para2: Maryland's fortune was tobacco. The crop spread plantations along every tidal creek of the Chesapeake, where ships could load hogsheads of cured leaf directly at plantation wharves. Tobacco was so central that it served as money: taxes, fines and wages were reckoned in pounds of leaf, and the colony built inspection warehouses to grade it. Great planters like the Carrolls amassed estates, but most tobacco was grown by small farmers leaning on the labor of indentured servants from England.
pageData.para3: The colony's labor order transformed over the century. Servants who survived their terms claimed land of their own, pushing up the Chesapeake's rivers and straining relations with Native neighbors, while elite rivalry and anti-Catholic resentment erupted in the 1689 'Protestant Revolution' that ended proprietary religious policy and made the Church of England Maryland's established church. After about 1690, as the supply of English servants dried up, planters turned decisively to enslaved Africans, and by the mid-eighteenth century slavery had replaced servitude as the foundation of Chesapeake tobacco society.
pageData.para4: Restored to the Calverts in 1715, Maryland matured into a prosperous, aristocratic province of brick courthouses, horse racing and vast river estates, its capital moved to the rising port of Annapolis. Its twin legacies, an early, fragile experiment in religious liberty and a society built on tobacco and, increasingly, enslaved labor, capture the contradictions of the colonial Chesapeake.

pageData.source3label: Library of Congress: Commerce in Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia

pageData.title: Colonial New England's Towns, Schools and Maritime Economy
pageData.titleline: Colonial New England's Towns, Schools and Maritime Economy - The History Web
pageData.para1: New England colonists did not scatter across the wilderness; they planted towns. Massachusetts and Connecticut granted land to groups of proprietors who laid out a meetinghouse and common pasture surrounded by family house lots, with outlying fields divided among them. The town was at once congregation, school district and government. Each year, men gathered in town meeting to elect selectmen and constables, vote taxes, assign roads and fence common land, a training ground in self-rule that made the New England town meeting a byword for grassroots democracy.
pageData.para2: Rocky soil and a short growing season pushed New Englanders to the sea. Fishing fleets took cod on the Grand Banks, colonial shipwrights built so many oceangoing vessels that by the eve of the Revolution at least a third of the British merchant fleet was American-built, and Yankee merchants carried lumber, fish, horses and provisions to the West Indies, returning with sugar and molasses to distill into rum. Boston, Newport and Portsmouth became Atlantic ports tied into the trade of three continents, while every tidewater village built its own vessels. New England's wealth floated on salt water.
pageData.para3: Congregational orthodoxy made reading essential: every believer was expected to read the Bible. Massachusetts required public schools by law from 1647, and literacy became widespread in the region. Harvard (1636) and Yale (1701) trained ministers, while town grammar schools and 'dame schools' taught children their letters. Printing presses in Boston and Cambridge poured out sermons, almanacs and primers, the New England Primer selling in the millions across the colonial era.
pageData.para4: By the eighteenth century the old Puritan unity was fraying. Prosperous port merchants, 'half-way' church memberships, the revivals of the Great Awakening and steady immigration diluted the founders' vision, even as town discipline endured. Yet the institutions of town, school and congregation remained the frame of daily life, and the habits they taught, meeting, voting, reading, arguing, would make New England a seedbed of revolution when crown and colony came into conflict.
pageData.source1label: Smithsonian NMAH: Within These Walls, a New England House
pageData.source2label: OpenStax U.S. History: English Settlements in America
pageData.source3label: National Park Service: Town of Churches, Boston

pageData.title: Colonial Assemblies and the Growth of Self-Government
pageData.titleline: Colonial Assemblies and the Growth of Self-Government - The History Web
pageData.para1: One of the most consequential developments of colonial America happened quietly, in committee rooms: the rise of elected assemblies. The first was Virginia's House of Burgesses, summoned in 1619, only twelve years after Jamestown's founding, when the Virginia Company allowed settlers a voice in their own laws. By the eve of the Revolution, elected assemblies had become a central institution of colonial government. Royal charters and governors might come and go, but the principle that Englishmen must consent to their own government had taken root in American soil and would not be pulled up.
pageData.para2: The assemblies' power grew from a simple lever: money. Governors were sent from London or appointed by proprietors, but their salaries and all local taxes had to be voted by the assemblies, and the 'power of the purse' proved mightier than royal instructions. Year after year, burgesses and representatives withheld salaries, rewrote money bills and traded appropriations for concessions, winning control over taxation, election rules, courts and much of colonial administration. Historians call the result the rise of the assembly, a slow constitutional revolution carried out by bookkeeping.
pageData.para3: These bodies were not democracies in the modern sense. Voting was generally limited to white men with property, and great planter and merchant families dominated the benches. But they were genuinely representative for their time, their members chosen in hard-fought local elections and answerable to neighbors. In their debates, a generation of American politicians, including Patrick Henry, Benjamin Franklin and John Dickinson, learned the arts of legislation, finance and opposition that would one day run a nation.
pageData.para4: When Britain tried to tax the colonies directly after 1763, it struck the assemblies' most sacred claim: that only they could tax their constituents. The cry of 'no taxation without representation' was not new doctrine but a summary of a century and a half of practice. The assemblies coordinated the resistance, the Stamp Act Congress, the committees of correspondence, that turned thirteen separate colonies into a united cause. America's revolution began in its colonial legislatures.
pageData.source3label: Encyclopedia.com: Colonial Government in British America

pageData.title: Colonial Printing, Newspapers and the Public Sphere
pageData.titleline: Colonial Printing, Newspapers and the Public Sphere - The History Web
pageData.para1: The first printing press in British North America arrived at Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1638, where Stephen Daye's shop produced the Bay Psalm Book of 1640, the first book printed in the English North American colonies. For a century, printing was a tightly held craft: a press required heavy capital, and authorities licensed printers, who made their living from government contracts, sermons, almanacs and blank forms. By 1700 presses worked in Boston, Cambridge, New York and Philadelphia; by the mid-eighteenth century, dozens of presses operated in colonial towns.
pageData.para2: Printing's great engine was the newspaper. The Boston News-Letter of 1704 was the first continuously published paper in America; by mid-century weeklies like Franklin's Pennsylvania Gazette and the Boston Gazette reached far beyond their cities. Newspapers carried shipping news, advertisements, essays and reprinted London politics, and printers swapped copies so that news jumped from colony to colony. In an age of bad roads, the post riders carrying papers stitched thirteen scattered colonies into a single conversation, creating what historians call a colonial public sphere.
pageData.para3: The press also tested the limits of power. In 1735 New York printer John Peter Zenger was tried for seditious libel after his newspaper attacked the royal governor. His lawyer Andrew Hamilton argued that truth should be a defense, and the jury's acquittal became an enduring landmark for freedom of the press, celebrated by generations of Americans. Colonial printers learned that their presses could challenge authority as well as serve it.
pageData.para4: When the imperial crisis came, print made it a shared cause. Printers spread the Stamp Act protests, serialized the patriotic essays of John Dickinson and Samuel Adams, and by the time shots were fired at Lexington in 1775, colonial newspapers and pamphlets had already created something new: an American public that read, argued and acted together. When Tom Paine's Common Sense appeared in January 1776, printers carried it to an unprecedented circulation, and its argument for independence ran through that public in a matter of weeks.
pageData.source2label: Smithsonian NMAH: The Franklin Common Press
pageData.source3label: Library of Congress: Chronicling America, Historic Newspapers

pageData.title: Indentured Servitude and Bacon's Rebellion
pageData.titleline: Indentured Servitude and Bacon's Rebellion - The History Web
pageData.para1: Seventeenth-century Virginia ran on bound labor. Most English immigrants arrived as indentured servants, signing contracts to work four to seven years for the master who paid their passage, in exchange for 'freedom dues,' often including land, at the end. Tens of thousands came; disease and overwork killed many before their terms ended, and those who survived increasingly found that the best tobacco land along the Chesapeake's rivers was already claimed by the great planter families who governed the colony. By the 1670s Virginia held a dangerous class: young, landless, armed freedmen with no future on the frontier's edge.
pageData.para2: The spark came from the frontier's violence. Colonists pressing onto Indigenous land clashed with the Susquehannock and other nations, and in 1675 a dispute over a debt spiraled into raids and reprisals. Frontier settlers demanded war, but Governor William Berkeley, protecting his own fur-trade interests and wary of all-out conflict, refused and authorized only defensive forts. To the frontier, this looked like betrayal by a distant, corrupt clique in Jamestown, the 'green spring faction' of Berkeley's cronies.
pageData.para3: Nathaniel Bacon, a young, charismatic, newly arrived member of the governor's own council, put himself at the head of the angry freedmen. In 1676 his volunteers attacked the peaceful Pamunkey and Occaneechi, enraging Berkeley, who declared Bacon a rebel. The quarrel became civil war: Bacon was elected to the assembly, arrested, released, and returned at the head of five hundred men to force a commission from the governor at gunpoint. When Berkeley fled across the Chesapeake, Bacon's army burned Jamestown to the ground in September 1676.
pageData.para4: The rebellion collapsed as suddenly as it rose. Bacon died of dysentery in October, his movement leaderless. Berkeley regained control and hanged twenty-three rebels. But the uprising changed Virginia. Planters drew a lasting lesson about the danger of a white servant underclass, and over the following decades they shifted decisively to enslaved African labor, sharpening racial law to divide poor whites from enslaved Blacks. Historians read Bacon's Rebellion as a turning point: the moment the Chesapeake's labor system and its racial order began to harden into their enduring form.
pageData.source3label: National Park Service: An Indigenous History of Bacon's Rebellion

pageData.title: The Stono Rebellion and Resistance to Colonial Slavery
pageData.titleline: The Stono Rebellion and Resistance to Colonial Slavery - The History Web
pageData.para1: On Sunday, September 9, 1739, near the Stono River south of Charles Town, about twenty enslaved Africans broke into a store, killed the two shopkeepers, and seized guns and powder. Led by a man remembered as Jemmy, likely from the Kongo region where many were Catholic and many had military experience, they marched south along the road toward Spanish Florida, where the crown had promised freedom to fugitives from the English colonies. Beating drums, flying a banner and calling out 'Liberty,' they gathered recruits as they went, burning plantations and killing some twenty to twenty-five whites who stood in their way.
pageData.para2: The rising burned for hours, not days. That afternoon the militia met the rebels, by then sixty to one hundred strong, at the Edisto River, and in the ensuing fight and weeks of pursuit most were killed or captured. Captured leaders were executed, their heads posted on mile markers as warning. Yet the rebels had come remarkably close to their aim: had they outrun the militia, the swamps and the Spanish border lay open before them.
pageData.para3: South Carolina's response was the Negro Act of 1740, one of the harshest slave codes in American history. It barred enslaved people from learning to read, assembling, raising their own food, or moving without a pass, restricted manumission, and tightened every screw of control, while also, on paper, limiting masters' cruelest punishments. The colony even briefly suspended the African slave trade. The act's long shadow shows how deeply Stono had frightened the slaveholding minority of a majority-Black colony.
pageData.para4: Stono was the largest slave rebellion in Britain's mainland colonies, but it was one current in a constant stream of resistance, from everyday defiance to conspiracies in New York and the Caribbean. It demonstrated that enslaved people understood the politics of empires, aiming deliberately for the Spanish promise of freedom, and that they would die fighting for liberty in a land that celebrated the word. The rebellion shaped the laws of the South for a century and remains a landmark in the long African American freedom struggle.
pageData.source2label: PBS Africans in America: The Stono Rebellion

pageData.title: King Philip's War
pageData.titleline: King Philip's War - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1675, two generations after the Mayflower, the alliance between the Wampanoag and the English collapsed into the bloodiest war per capita in American history. Metacom, called King Philip by the English, was the son of Massasoit, the sachem who had made peace with Plymouth in 1621. By his time the balance had shifted utterly: colonial towns had multiplied, Native land had been fenced for farms and herds, and Native people were being dragged before English courts under English law. When three Wampanoag were tried and hanged for the murder of John Sassamon, a Christian Native informant, in June 1675, warriors attacked Swansea, and New England ignited.
pageData.para2: The war that followed was a war of whole peoples. Colonial militia marched against Metacom's homeland at Mount Hope, forcing the Wampanoag into flight and alliance-building; the colonists' demand that the neutral Narragansett surrender fugitives backfired, driving that powerful nation into the war. In December 1675, a thousand colonial troops stormed the Narragansett winter fort in the Great Swamp Fight, killing hundreds of women, children and elders. Through the bitter winter, Native forces struck back, burning town after town: Lancaster, Medfield, Groton, and more than half of New England's settlements were attacked.
pageData.para3: Spring turned the tide. Native forces, short of gunpowder, food and allies, could not plant their corn, while colonial troops, now allied with the Mohegan, Pequot and Mohawk, hunted the war parties down. Metacom's support melted away; his wife and son were captured in August 1676, and days later he was cornered in a swamp and shot by an Indigenous soldier serving with the English. His head was displayed on a pole at Plymouth for twenty years. His wife and child were sold into slavery in the West Indies.
pageData.para4: King Philip's War destroyed Native power in southern New England. Several thousand Native people were dead, enslaved or driven from their homelands, and the survivors were confined to small praying towns and reservations. But it nearly destroyed New England too: a dozen towns lay in ashes, one in ten military-age colonial men was dead, and the economy took a generation to recover. The war remains a landmark of what colonial expansion cost, and for the Wampanoag and their neighbors, a catastrophe survived but never forgotten.

pageData.title: The Garifuna: Displacement, Resistance and Identity
pageData.titleline: The Garifuna: Displacement, Resistance and Identity - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Garifuna people were forged in resistance on the island of St. Vincent in the eastern Caribbean. In the seventeenth century Africans - shipwrecked, escaped, or brought by trade - found refuge among the island's Kalinago, the Island Caribs, and from their union emerged the community the British called the Black Caribs, who kept the Arawak-derived language and much of the culture of their Indigenous forebears while absorbing African heritage. By the eighteenth century they held most of St. Vincent, farming, trading, and refusing both European powers' claims to their land.
pageData.para2: Britain and France fought over St. Vincent for decades, but Britain's drive to expand plantations brought conflict with the Garifuna. Under Joseph Chatoyer, the Black Caribs resisted in the Second Carib War of 1795-96. Chatoyer was killed in March 1795, but resistance continued until British forces defeated the Garifuna in 1796. From July of that year, British authorities rounded up thousands of men, women, and children and confined them on Balliceaux, where many died from disease and harsh conditions. In 1797 the surviving exiles were sent to Roatán in the Bay of Honduras.
pageData.para3: From Roatán the exiles crossed to the mainland coast in 1797, landing first near Trujillo in Honduras, and from there they spread along the Caribbean shore of Central America. Welcomed by the Spanish as farmers and soldiers, they settled the coasts of what became Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala, and Belize, famed as fishermen, cassava farmers, and the finest boatmen of the coast. Wherever they landed they rebuilt their towns - Dangriga, Livingston, Tela, Orinoco - carrying with them the seeds, songs, and rites of St. Vincent.
pageData.para4: The Garifuna kept their identity alive across three nations and two centuries. Their language still bears the imprint of the Island Carib world; their punta music, wanaragua dances, and the dügü ritual, in which the ancestors are called, sustain the culture of exile. A people Britain tried to erase in 1797 had, by the early twentieth century, become an unbroken thread of Indigenous and African survival along the entire Central American coast.

pageData.title: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680
pageData.titleline: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680 - The History Web
pageData.para1: In August 1680, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico carried out the most successful Indigenous uprising in North American colonial history. Spain had ruled the region for eighty years: Franciscan missions demanded conversion and suppressed the katsina religion, while soldiers and settlers seized land, food and labor under the encomienda system. Pueblo communities endured drought, Apache raids and epidemics, and when authorities hanged accused 'sorcerers' and publicly whipped dozens of religious leaders in 1675, among them a Tewa man from San Juan named Po'pay, resistance hardened into a plan.
pageData.para2: Po'pay and other leaders organized a coordinated rising across dozens of scattered pueblos speaking six different languages. Runners carried knotted cords marking the days until the attack, and despite Spanish efforts to intercept them, on August 10, 1680, warriors struck missions and farms almost simultaneously, killing some 400 colonists and 21 friars. Survivors fled to the fortified capital of Santa Fe, which the Pueblos besieged until Governor Antonio de Otermin and about two thousand refugees abandoned the province, marching south down the Rio Grande to El Paso.
pageData.para3: For twelve years, New Mexico was again governed by its own peoples. The victors destroyed churches, baptized away Christian names, and revived suppressed ceremonies. Po'pay's attempt to restore a pre-conquest order proved harder to sustain than the revolt itself: drought returned, Apache and Ute raiding pressed the weakened pueblos, and old rivalries resurfaced, fragmenting the alliance he had built. Spanish exiles in El Paso never abandoned hope of return.
pageData.para4: In 1692 Diego de Vargas led a bloodless reentry, and over four years Spain reconquered the province, this time on new terms. Chastened officials curbed the encomienda, tolerated more Pueblo religious life, and treated the pueblos as negotiating partners rather than subjects to be crushed. The revolt's deepest legacy is that it worked: it preserved Pueblo languages, lands and religion. The pueblos carried their self-government forward under the settlement that followed, and the memory of 1680 endured as standing proof that empire in the Southwest ruled only by Pueblo consent.

pageData.title: Spanish Florida and St. Augustine
pageData.titleline: Spanish Florida and St. Augustine - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1565, the Spanish captain-general Pedro Menendez de Aviles founded St. Augustine on Florida's Atlantic coast, the oldest continuously occupied European-established city in the continental United States. His orders were strategic: drive out a rival French colony at Fort Caroline, which he destroyed within weeks, and anchor Spain's claim to La Florida, the vast territory guarding the route of the treasure fleets. As galleons heavy with Mexican and Peruvian silver rode the Gulf Stream home along Florida's shore, St. Augustine became the military sentinel of the richest shipping lane in the world.
pageData.para2: Spanish Florida was always more frontier mission province than settler colony. A chain of Franciscan missions spread among the Timucua, Guale and Apalachee peoples, whose chiefs often allied with Spain for trade goods and protection, building a biracial society of soldiers, friars, farmers and Native towns. The colony also became a beacon for the enslaved: after 1693 the Spanish crown offered freedom to fugitives from English Carolina who accepted baptism, and in 1738 free Black settlers founded Fort Mose near St. Augustine, the first legally sanctioned free African town in what is now the United States.
pageData.para3: Because wooden forts had failed before pirates and enemies, Spain began the Castillo de San Marcos in 1672, a star-shaped fortress of coquina, a local shellstone that absorbed cannonballs instead of shattering. The Castillo proved its worth in 1702 and again in 1740, when English forces from South Carolina and Georgia besieged St. Augustine and battered the fort without taking it. During the Seven Years' War Havana fell, and in the 1763 peace Spain traded all Florida to Britain for its return, ending two centuries of Spanish rule.
pageData.para4: Britain held Florida for twenty years, dividing it into East and West Florida, before the American Revolution returned it to Spain in 1783. Weakened Spain could not hold the province against American settlers, filibusters and Seminoles, and in 1819 agreed the Adams-Onis Treaty, handing Florida to the United States in 1821. But St. Augustine's oldest houses, its fortress, and the mixed Spanish, Native and African heritage of its people still mark the nation's oldest colonial city.

pageData.title: The Atlantic Slave Trade and Slavery in British North America
pageData.titleline: The Atlantic Slave Trade and Slavery in British North America - The History Web
pageData.para1: Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, European traders carried between ten and twelve million Africans across the Atlantic in chains, one of the largest forced migrations in human history. Britain became the trade's greatest carrier, its ships sailing a triangular route: manufactured goods to West Africa, captives to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco and cotton home. On the Middle Passage, captives were packed below decks in filth and disease; roughly one in seven died at sea. This was not an incidental evil but the economic engine of the Atlantic world, and British North America stood within it.
pageData.para2: The first Africans in the English mainland colonies, 'twenty and odd' captives, were landed at Virginia in 1619, into a society where their status was at first ambiguous, and some early Africans won freedom and property. Over the seventeenth century, however, colonial law closed around them. As planters shifted from indentured servants to enslaved Africans, statutes made slavery hereditary through the mother and permanent for life. By 1700, colonial statutes treated the great majority of Black colonists as enslaved property, though free Black people still lived in every region.
pageData.para3: By the eighteenth century, slavery anchored entire regional economies. In the Chesapeake, enslaved workers grew tobacco; in the South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry, they built and worked the rice and indigo plantations, their African skills essential to the crop; in the North, enslaved people labored on farms, in ports and in households, and northern merchants profited from slave-traded goods. By 1775 some 500,000 people of African descent lived in the thirteen colonies, a fifth of the population, the great majority enslaved.
pageData.para4: Enslaved people resisted the system in every way open to them: work slowdowns, escape, the preservation of African family, faith and culture in the face of systematic dehumanization, and open rebellion from New York in 1712 to Stono in 1739. Their labor built colonial wealth, their presence shaped colonial law, and the contradiction between the colonists' language of liberty and the reality of slavery would haunt the nation they were about to found.

pageData.title: The Homestead Act and the Transformation of the West
pageData.para1: On May 20, 1862, in the midst of the Civil War, President Lincoln signed the Homestead Act, the fulfillment of a generation of demands for free land. The law offered any adult citizen or intended citizen, including women, freedpeople, and immigrants, title to 160 acres of public land in exchange for a small filing fee, five years of residence, and improvements to the claim. Southern opposition to free homesteads had blocked the idea for decades; secession removed it. Together with the Morrill land-grant college act and the Pacific Railway Act, passed the same year, the Homestead Act turned the federal government into an engine of western development.
pageData.para2: Homesteading was brutally hard. On the treeless plains settlers cut sod for houses, burned buffalo chips for fuel, and watched drought, blizzards, and grasshopper swarms destroy their crops; the barbed wire invented in 1874 let farmers fence fields and finally hold the open range. Many families failed and sold out. Land speculators and railroads used dummy claims and legal loopholes to amass land that was meant for settlers. Yet the law worked: the peak year of homestead claims was 1913, when settlers filed on eleven million acres of the public domain in a single year.
pageData.para3: The land was not empty. The plains and prairies belonged to Indigenous nations whose treaties were made and broken as settlement advanced. The same decades brought the Sand Creek massacre of 1864, the destruction of the buffalo that underpinned plains economies, the reservation system, and the wars recounted on the Plains Indian Wars page. In 1887 the Dawes Act broke tribal lands into individual allotments, stripping Indigenous nations of much of their remaining land. The homestead frontier and Indigenous dispossession were two faces of the same transformation.
pageData.para4: By 1890 the census declared the frontier line gone, and in 1893 the historian Frederick Jackson Turner argued that free land had shaped American democracy and character. The wheat and cattle kingdoms the homesteaders and ranchers built fed the industrial East and the world, and homesteading continued on ever more marginal land into the twentieth century, with enlarged claims for dryland farming. Its formative era belongs to the generation after 1862, and by 1924 the homestead frontier it created had become the agricultural heart of the nation.

pageData.title: Industrialization, Big Business and the Gilded Age
pageData.para1: In the four decades after the Civil War, the United States became the world's leading industrial nation. The raw materials were there: coal, iron ore, oil, timber, and the farm output of a continent. So were the people, millions of immigrants and farm youth flowing into factory cities, and the capital, supplied by banks and by the profits of war. Railroads, covered on their own page, tied it all into the largest free-trade market on earth, while protective tariffs, cheap public land, and a government friendly to enterprise kept the conditions favorable. Between 1860 and 1900 American manufacturing output multiplied many times over, and by 1900 it surpassed Britain's.
pageData.para2: New technologies made new industries. The Bessemer process made steel cheap, and Andrew Carnegie built an empire on it, controlling every stage from ore to rail before selling out to J. P. Morgan's United States Steel in 1901, the first billion-dollar corporation. John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil refined and distributed most of the nation's kerosene, organizing competitors into a trust that the courts eventually ordered dissolved in 1911. Electricity lit the cities through Edison's and Westinghouse's systems, the telephone and typewriter remade business, and meatpacking, milling, and machinery became industries on a continental scale. Business leaders defended their power with the language of Social Darwinism and Carnegie's own Gospel of Wealth, which argued the rich should give away their fortunes for the public good.
pageData.para3: Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner named the era in their 1873 novel The Gilded Age: a surface of glitter over base metal. Industrial fortunes built mansions on Fifth Avenue while tenement families, described on the Immigration and Urban America page, crowded a few blocks away. Corruption reached from Tammany Hall's Tweed Ring in New York to the Credit Mobilier scandal in Congress. Workers labored ten or twelve hours a day, six days a week, in mines and mills where death and injury were routine, and their answer, organization and strikes, is told on the Labor Movement page.
pageData.para4: The pressures of industrial capitalism produced the first efforts at national regulation: the Interstate Commerce Commission of 1887 and the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 were weak beginnings, but beginnings. After 1900 the Progressive movement, drawing on the agrarian protest covered on the Populism page, pushed regulation much further, breaking up trusts, pure food and drug laws, and new protections for workers and consumers. By 1924 the United States was an industrial colossus whose factories produced nearly half the world's manufactures, a transformation unimaginable when the Civil War began.
