pageData.title: The American Labor Movement and the Great Strikes
pageData.para1: Industrial workers in Gilded Age America faced long hours, subsistence wages, child labor, and machines that maimed thousands every year, with no insurance, no pensions, and courts ready to jail organizers. Their answer was combination. The National Labor Union, founded in 1866, campaigned for the eight-hour day; the Knights of Labor, organized in 1869 and led after 1879 by Terence Powderly, welcomed nearly all producers, skilled and unskilled, men and women, Black and white, into one big union, and swelled to perhaps seven hundred thousand members by 1886. The Knights dreamed of a cooperative commonwealth, but their future was decided in the strike waves of the 1870s and 1880s.
pageData.para2: The Great Railroad Strike of 1877 was the first nationwide labor conflict in American history. When the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad cut wages for the second time in a year, workers in West Virginia walked out, and the strike spread along the rail lines to Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Chicago, and St. Louis. State militia killed strikers, crowds burned rail yards, and President Hayes sent federal troops to move the trains. Perhaps a hundred people died before the strike collapsed. It failed, but it announced that labor conflict in industrial America would be national, and often violent.
pageData.para3: In May 1886 a nationwide campaign for the eight-hour day ended at Chicago's Haymarket Square, where a bomb thrown at police killed seven officers; eight anarchist leaders were convicted in a trial widely condemned as unjust, and four were hanged. The Knights of Labor, unfairly tarred by the bombing, went into decline, and leadership passed to the American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886 under Samuel Gompers, which organized skilled workers by craft and pursued wages and hours rather than utopia. The 1890s brought the era's bitterest defeats: troops broke the Homestead steel strike against Carnegie in 1892, and in 1894 the government used a court injunction and the army to crush the Pullman boycott led by Eugene V. Debs's American Railway Union.
pageData.para4: Labor's fortunes rose slowly after 1900. The AFL grew to millions of members, the mine workers won recognition in the coal fields, and the great strike wave of 1919, followed by the open-shop drive of the 1920s, showed both the movement's reach and its limits. Courts, troops, and hostile law remained labor's constant enemies, but the union idea was permanent, and the eight-hour day, won industry by industry, was written into federal law for railroad workers in 1916.

pageData.title: The Red Summer of 1919 and Racial Violence
pageData.titleline: The Red Summer of 1919 and Racial Violence - The History Web
pageData.para1: The summer and autumn of 1919 saw the worst outbreak of racial violence in American history to that time. Black veterans were returning from the First World War determined to claim the democracy they had fought for; Black workers who had migrated north for war jobs competed with whites for housing and work; and lynching, 64 victims in 1918 and 83 in 1919, kept pace. In more than three dozen cities and one rural county in Arkansas, white mobs attacked Black communities. Black Americans, many of them armed veterans, fought back, notably in Washington, D.C., and Chicago. The writer James Weldon Johnson gave the season its name: the Red Summer.
pageData.para2: The worst urban riot began in Chicago on July 27, 1919, when a Black teenager, Eugene Williams, swimming in Lake Michigan, drifted across an invisible racial boundary at a segregated beach and was stoned and drowned. When police refused to arrest the white man blamed, crowds gathered, distorted rumors swept the city, and for days gangs fought through the South Side despite the calling out of the state militia. By the end, 38 people were dead, 23 of them Black, hundreds were injured, and a thousand Black families were left homeless by arson.
pageData.para3: Violence took different forms elsewhere. In Washington, D.C., white soldiers and sailors attacked Black neighborhoods until residents organized their own defense. In Omaha, a mob stormed a courthouse and lynched a Black prisoner. In Elaine, Arkansas, Black sharecroppers who had met to organize a union were attacked, and in the massacre and reprisals that followed, scores, perhaps hundreds, of Black people were killed, the deadliest episode of all.
pageData.para4: The Red Summer exposed the cost of asking Black Americans to fight abroad for freedoms denied at home, and it changed Black politics. The NAACP grew rapidly as it publicized and investigated the violence, and a new spirit of open resistance, soon voiced by the poets and organizers of the 1920s, took hold. The violence of 1919 remained a raw memory in 1924 and a warning of what unresolved injustice could ignite.

pageData.title: The Numbered Treaties of Canada
pageData.titleline: The Numbered Treaties of Canada - The History Web
pageData.para1: Between 1871 and 1921 the Crown concluded eleven agreements with First Nations across northern and western Canada, known from their numbering as the Numbered Treaties. The process began as soon as Canada acquired Rupert's Land: before the prairies could be surveyed, settled, and crossed by the promised railway, the government needed to extinguish Indigenous title under the framework of the Royal Proclamation of 1763. Treaties 1 and 2 were made in Manitoba in 1871, Treaty 3 at the North-West Angle of the Lake of the Woods in 1873, Treaty 4 at Fort Qu'Appelle in 1874, Treaties 5 and 6 across the Saskatchewan country in 1875-76, and Treaty 7 with the Blackfoot Confederacy at Blackfoot Crossing in 1877; Treaties 8 to 11, from 1899 to 1921, extended the system into the northern forests and the Mackenzie valley.
pageData.para2: The written texts followed a pattern: First Nations 'ceded, released and surrendered' vast territories in return for reserve lands, small annual payments, ammunition and twine, farming tools and seed, and schooling when desired; Treaty 6 added a medicine chest and a promise of famine relief. But the treaties were made between two worlds. First Nations leaders negotiated through interpreters, sealed the agreements with sacred ceremonies, and understood them as covenants of peace and shared land - an ongoing relationship with the Queen - while the Crown's lawyers understood a permanent, one-time surrender of territory. Much of what commissioners such as Alexander Morris promised orally never reached the written page.
pageData.para3: The hard years came fast. The buffalo, the foundation of plains life, were gone by the early 1880s, and Ottawa exploited the hunger that followed, withholding food to push holdout bands into treaty and onto reserves - a policy even some of its own officials called cruel. Big Bear held out against Treaty 6 until 1882, the last major plains chief to sign. After the 1885 resistance, which some treaty bands joined, the government imposed controls found nowhere in the treaties: a pass system restricting movement off reserves, cuts to rations and tools, and a 'peasant farming' policy that kept reserve agriculture small. Leaders like Poundmaker were imprisoned and humiliated, and promised famine aid arrived late or never.
pageData.para4: Through 1921 the treaty map was completed northward, and by the early 1920s nearly all First Nations of the west lived under their terms. For the settler state the treaties had cleared the way for the railway, the wheat boom, and the provinces carved from the territories; for First Nations they had brought reserves, disease, and control, but also a set of solemn promises they never abandoned. Treaty days, when the annual payments were distributed, became occasions to renew that relationship and to press, year after year, for the Crown to keep its word.

pageData.title: The US Occupation of Haiti, 1915-1924
pageData.titleline: The US Occupation of Haiti, 1915-1924 - The History Web
pageData.para1: On 28 July 1915 United States Marines landed in Port-au-Prince, beginning a military occupation of Haiti. Washington had watched Haiti's chronic instability with growing impatience: since 1911 the republic had seen seven presidents, and the immediate pretext came when a mob killed President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam after he had ordered the massacre of political prisoners. Behind the pretext lay strategy - fear that Germany, whose merchants dominated Haitian trade, might gain a base near the Panama Canal in wartime - and finance: the National City Bank of New York had acquired Haiti's national bank, and in December 1914, months before the landing, American Marines had already carried half a million dollars of the republic's gold reserve aboard the USS Machias to New York.
pageData.para2: The occupation remade the Haitian state by force. The United States imposed a treaty giving it control of Haiti's finances, customs, and police; dissolved the army and replaced it with an American-officered gendarmerie; and in 1918 pushed through a new constitution, drafted with the help of the young assistant Navy secretary Franklin Roosevelt, that struck down the old ban on foreign landownership. When Haiti's legislature balked at the constitution, the Americans had it dissolved, and President Philippe Sudré Dartiguenave ruled by decree.
pageData.para3: Haitians resisted in arms. The corvée - forced labour gangs building the occupation's roads - revived memories of slavery and provoked the great uprising of the cacos, the country fighters of the north, under Charlemagne Péralte, a former gendarmerie officer who deserted to lead them. From 1918 to 1920 Péralte's army of thousands fought the Marines and gendarmerie across the countryside, until he was betrayed and killed in October 1919; his body, photographed crucified against a door, became a martyr's icon. Benoît Batraville kept the rebellion alive until his death in 1920. Thousands of Haitians died in the suppression.
pageData.para4: Through 1924 the occupation ground on under the treaty of 1915: roads were built, the budget balanced, sanitation improved, and elections choreographed by the American high command, which governed in partnership with a small elite while censoring the press and jailing critics. The occupation deepened the colour and class divisions of Haitian life, centralized power in Port-au-Prince at the expense of the countryside, and provoked a nationalist and noiriste intellectual awakening.

pageData.title: Cuba's Early Republic and the Platt Amendment, 1902-1924
pageData.titleline: Cuba's Early Republic and the Platt Amendment, 1902-1924 - The History Web
pageData.para1: On 20 May 1902 the United States military government lowered its flag and Tomás Estrada Palma, the veteran of the independence wars, was inaugurated as first president of the Republic of Cuba. The independence Cubans had fought for through thirty years of war came with strings: the Platt Amendment, passed by the US Congress in 1901 and forced into Cuba's constitution as the price of withdrawal, gave the United States the right to intervene in Cuban affairs, control over Cuba's foreign and financial relations, and the lease of naval bases at Guantánamo Bay. Cuba was sovereign in name and a protectorate in fact, its independence, as the amendment's critics said, held on deposit in Washington.
pageData.para2: The Platt framework was used early and often. Fraud and violence in the 1905 elections drove the opposition Liberals to revolt in 1906, and President Roosevelt dispatched troops in the 'Second Occupation', governing Cuba through Charles Magoon until 1909. United States forces landed again in 1912 when the Partido Independiente de Color, the party of Black veterans who found the republic's promises of equality unfulfilled, rose in protest and was crushed in a campaign in which thousands of Afro-Cubans were killed. Washington's Marines protected an economy in which American capital poured into sugar mills, railroads, and utilities until US interests dominated the island's life.
pageData.para3: Sugar made and unmade the early republic. The world war drove prices to a giddy peak in the 'Dance of the Millions' of 1920, when Cuban sugar sold at over twenty-two cents a pound and Havana bankers bought banks with loans - then collapsed to four cents, ruining planters, banks, and the treasury, and drawing American banks deeper into Cuban finance. Presidents came and went under Washington's eye: José Miguel Gómez, Mario García Menocal - re-elected in 1916 amid fraud that the United States had to referee - and, from 1921, Alfredo Zayas, whose government Washington tutored through an 'honest cabinet' imposed by its envoy Enoch Crowder.
pageData.para4: By 1924 the early republic had settled into its pattern: sugar monoculture chained to the American market, politics managed between Havana's factions and the American embassy, and the Guantánamo base a permanent symbol of the Platt settlement. Yet the period also bred its own answer: a generation of students, veterans, and nationalists who measured the republic against José Martí's dream of Cuba libre.

pageData.title: Costa Rica's Coffee Economy and Liberal State
pageData.titleline: Costa Rica's Coffee Economy and Liberal State - The History Web
pageData.para1: Costa Rica became a major Central American coffee exporter. After independence in 1821, settlers in the central highlands found that the volcanic soils around San Jose, Heredia, Alajuela, and Cartago suited the crop, and the state gave land and tax privileges to anyone who would plant it. Shipments to London began in the 1840s, and coffee soon paid for roads, schools, and public buildings. Because colonial Costa Rica had been poor and thinly populated, with few great estates, coffee wealth spread more widely among small and medium farmers than elsewhere in the isthmus, though processors and exporters captured the largest profits.
pageData.para2: The liberal state took shape under General Tomas Guardia, who seized power in 1870 and dominated politics until his death in 1882. His governments wrote the constitution of 1871, curbed the church, promoted education, and signed a contract with the American railroad builder Minor Keith to link the highlands to the Caribbean. The Atlantic railway, finished in 1890, placed a heavy burden on public finances but carried coffee to Europe, and the lands granted to Keith along the line became the base of a banana industry that later fed into the United Fruit Company. In 1889 the government of Bernardo Soto tried to impose his successor, but public protests forced it to respect the vote, an event Costa Ricans remember as the birth of their democracy.
pageData.para3: Coffee society rested on the work of the whole country. Each harvest, families from the highlands picked the crop, and the famous painted oxcarts carried the beans down to the Pacific port of Puntarenas. Processors in San Jose, the beneficios, cleaned and graded the coffee and advanced credit, wielding great power over small growers. Public investment in primary education was an important part of the liberal state, although access remained unequal.
pageData.para4: The system was not immune to crisis. Falling coffee prices after 1900 strained the treasury, and in 1917 the war minister Federico Tinoco seized power in a military coup. Popular opposition and American non-recognition forced him out in 1919, and constitutional rule returned with the election of Julio Acosta in 1920. By 1924 coffee exports and constitutional politics had become central to Costa Rican public life, though the banana enclave on the Atlantic coast, run by a foreign company with its own labor force, stood apart from the highland society that coffee had built.

pageData.title: El Salvador's Coffee Republic
pageData.titleline: El Salvador's Coffee Republic - The History Web
pageData.para1: In the mid-nineteenth century El Salvador's export economy rested on indigo, and when synthetic dyes undercut demand for natural indigo after the 1860s, the country's landowners turned to coffee. The volcanic highlands of the west were ideal for the crop, but much of that land belonged to Indigenous communities that held it in common. To clear the way for coffee estates, the liberal government of Rafael Zaldivar decreed the abolition of communal and municipal lands in 1881 and 1882. Within a generation, many community holdings were divided, transferred, or enclosed, and thousands of families became landless wage workers.
pageData.para2: The land laws provoked fierce resistance. Indigenous communities protested, petitioned, and at times rose in local revolts, which the army suppressed. To enforce the new order the state created rural police forces, and later, in 1912, a National Guard that answered to the planters. Vagrancy laws obliged landless workers to carry employment documents and pushed them onto the coffee estates during harvest. A small group of families came to control the best land, the banks, and the export trade, forming an oligarchy so concentrated that outsiders spoke of the fourteen families who ran the country.
pageData.para3: Coffee remade El Salvador's landscape and society. Shade-grown estates spread over the western volcanoes, railways linked the interior to the port of Acajutla, and the crop supplied the great majority of export earnings. The elite invested their profits in San Salvador's parks, theaters, and European-style buildings, presenting their country as an orderly, modern republic. In 1895 El Salvador joined Honduras and Nicaragua in the short-lived Greater Republic of Central America, an attempt at union that collapsed within three years, and thereafter the coffee elite concentrated on guarding their position at home.
pageData.para4: After the assassination of President Manuel Enrique Araujo in 1913, the presidency came under the control of the related Melendez and Quinonez families. Through the early 1920s their dominance gave the oligarchic system a surface stability. The state depended on coffee revenues, and planters relied on the state to discipline labor. Beneath the calm, landlessness and poverty deepened in the countryside. By 1924 coffee dominated export earnings, while Indigenous communities continued to defend their lands, institutions, and traditions under severe pressure.

pageData.title: Immigration Restriction and the Johnson-Reed Act of 1924
pageData.titleline: Immigration Restriction and the Johnson-Reed Act of 1924 - The History Web
pageData.para1: Between 1880 and 1914, more than twenty million immigrants came to the United States, most of them now from southern and eastern Europe: Italians, Poles, Jews, Greeks, and Slavs. The newcomers filled the factories and cities, but they also met rising nativism. Old-stock Americans, influenced by pseudoscientific theories of race, argued that the new immigrants could never be assimilated, and organized labor complained of competition for jobs. Congress responded first with a literacy test in 1917 and with an 'Asiatic Barred Zone' excluding most Asian immigrants.
pageData.para2: The First World War and the Red Scare turned restriction into a landslide cause. In 1921 Congress passed the Emergency Quota Act, capping annual immigration at about 350,000 and limiting each nationality to three percent of its foreign-born population in the 1910 census. President Harding signed it, but restrictionists wanted a sharper and more permanent cut.
pageData.para3: The Immigration Act of 1924, known as the Johnson-Reed Act, delivered it. The law lowered each nationality's quota to two percent and, crucially, moved the base year back from 1910 to 1890, before the great wave of southern and eastern European migration, so that the vast majority of visas went to northern and western Europeans. It banned virtually all immigration from Asia, provoking anger in Japan. Immigration from Canada and Latin America, however, was left outside the quota system.
pageData.para4: The effect was dramatic: immigration fell to a fraction of its prewar level, and the doors that had stood open for generations swung shut. The 1924 act became the cornerstone of American immigration policy as the era closed, and its national-origins logic marked the high point of the nativism that the war years and the Red Scare had unleashed.

pageData.title: The Whiskey Rebellion and Federal Authority, 1791-1794
pageData.titleline: The Whiskey Rebellion and Federal Authority, 1791-1794 - The History Web
pageData.para1: In 1791 Congress passed an excise tax on distilled spirits, the first internal tax laid by the new federal government. Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton wanted the revenue to reduce debts left over from the Revolutionary War and to assert national authority. On the western frontier the tax landed hard. Small farmers distilled their grain into whiskey because it was easier to ship and keep than bulk grain, and it also served as an informal currency. Many settlers saw the tax as a burden placed on them by eastern elites.
pageData.para2: Resistance began with refusals to pay and with attacks on revenue officers, who were sometimes tarred and feathered. In 1792 President George Washington issued a proclamation warning against resistance to the law. The protests turned violent in July 1794, when several hundred armed men near Pittsburgh burned the home of John Neville, the regional tax inspector. Protesters then gathered on Braddock's Field outside the city, and some talked of attacking the federal garrison there.
pageData.para3: Washington first tried negotiation. A committee of western representatives, which included Albert Gallatin, met commissioners without settling the crisis. In August 1794 Washington issued a proclamation ordering the insurgents home and called up militia from Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland and Virginia. About 13,000 men marched west, and Washington accompanied them for part of the way. The painting on this page, attributed to Frederick Kemmelmeyer and made after 1795, shows him reviewing the troops at Fort Cumberland, Maryland. By the time the army reached the region the opposition had dispersed and no battle took place.
pageData.para4: About 150 men were arrested, but weak evidence and missing witnesses hampered the trials. Two men, John Mitchell and Philip Weigel, were convicted of treason, and Washington pardoned both. Federalists took the outcome as proof that the national government could enforce its laws inside the states. Many Jeffersonian Republicans were alarmed by the size of the force and feared that central power was growing too strong. The dispute fed the political divisions of the 1790s, and the whiskey excise was repealed in 1802 under President Thomas Jefferson.

pageData.title: The Great Migration, 1916-1924
pageData.titleline: The Great Migration, 1916-1924 - The History Web
pageData.imagealt: The Negro Exodus from North Carolina: Scene at a Railway Station, wood engraving by W. L. Sheppard, Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper, 15 February 1890
pageData.para1: In 1900 nearly eight million Black people, about 90 percent of all Black Americans, lived in the South. Many were trapped in sharecropping and other forms of debt peonage, kept in an inferior position by Jim Crow laws and denied political rights. From 1916 a growing number left for cities in the North and West in search of work and an escape from racial violence. Wikipedia gives a conservative estimate of 400,000 Black Southerners leaving between 1916 and 1918.
pageData.para2: Several pressures combined. Farm failures and crop damage from the boll weevil added to the poverty of the rural South. The First World War slowed European immigration, and a military draft began in 1917, so Northern factories, foundries and slaughterhouses faced labor shortages. Black newspapers helped carry the news. Robert S. Abbott's Chicago Defender published train schedules, songs and cartoons, called the North a promised land, and carried job listings, and papers such as the Amsterdam News and the Pittsburgh Courier did the same for their own cities.
pageData.para3: The engraving on this page, published in Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper in 1890, shows Black families leaving North Carolina by rail. It records an earlier movement than the one described here. Northern cities were not free of discrimination. Migrants met segregated housing and schools, poor working conditions and low pay, and sometimes violence. The East St. Louis riot of 1917 killed between 40 and 200 Black residents, according to Wikipedia. In the Red Summer of 1919, racial violence spread through at least 26 cities.
pageData.para4: The Chicago riot of 1919 killed 38 people, 23 Black and 15 white, injured 537 and left about 1,000 Black families homeless. Black veterans of the war were among those who fought back. Even so, the movement changed the cities that received migrants. Between 1910 and 1920 the number of Black workers in industry nearly doubled, from 500,000 to 901,000. The Immigration Act of 1924 later cut European immigration further. This page covers only the first wave, to 1924. The Great Migration continued until 1970, and an estimated six million people took part over its whole course.

pageData.title: The Pequot War, 1636-1638
pageData.titleline: The Pequot War, 1636-1638 - The History Web
pageData.imagealt: Woodcut of the attack on the Pequot fort at Mystic, from John Underhill's Newes from America, London, 1638
pageData.para1: The Pequot War was fought in 1636 and 1637 between the Pequot people and a coalition of English settlers from the Massachusetts Bay, Connecticut and Saybrook colonies, joined by Native allies including the Narragansett and Mohegan. Its root was a struggle over the fur and wampum trade of the Connecticut River valley. Britannica notes that by 1635 the Pequot had extended control over modern Connecticut and eastern Long Island and headed a confederacy of dozens of tribes. Before the English arrived, the Dutch and the Pequot controlled the region's trade, and the tribes the Pequot had subjugated resented them and sought alliances with the English.
pageData.para2: The killing of English traders, John Stone in 1634 and John Oldham in 1636, became the immediate cause of war, though Britannica stresses that those deaths came after decades of conflict among Native peoples that the Dutch and English made worse. In late August 1636 Massachusetts Bay sent about ninety soldiers under John Endecott to Block Island and Pequot territory, where they burned villages and cornfields. The Pequot then besieged the fort at Saybrook from September 1636 to April 1637. After a Pequot attack on Wethersfield, the first time women and children were killed in the war, Connecticut declared war on May 1, 1637.
pageData.para3: Captain John Mason of Windsor was ordered to conduct an offensive war. In May 1637, in what Britannica calls the Mistick Campaign, he led English, Mohegan and Narragansett forces against the main fortified Pequot village at Mistick, in present-day Mystic, Connecticut. The attackers burned the village. Around 400 Pequot men, women and children were burned alive or killed. The woodcut on this page comes from John Underhill's 1638 account of the attack. It is a schematic print and shows the fort as a circle, not a realistic scene. The last battle of the war was the Swamp Fight at Fairfield, Connecticut.
pageData.para4: The Pequot were defeated and their communities scattered. The 1638 Treaty of Hartford outlawed the Pequot language and name, seized tribal lands and disbanded the survivors, who were given to the victors or sold into slavery. The English claimed all Pequot territory by right of conquest, and the war cleared the way for further English colonization of southern New England. Britannica calls it an especially brutal war and the first sustained conflict between Native Americans and Europeans in northeastern North America. The Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation in southeastern Connecticut is, in ConnecticutHistory.org's words, proof of a people's endurance.

pageData.title: The Powhatan Confederacy and English Colonization
pageData.titleline: The Powhatan Confederacy and English Colonization - The History Web
pageData.imagealt: Powhatan (Wahunsenacawh), paramount chief of the Powhatan Confederacy, in an 1880 engraving from Henry Clay Watson, A History of the United States (an imagined 19th-century likeness)
pageData.para1: Before the English arrived, Virginia Indians had lived in what is now Virginia for over 12,000 years. In May 1607 Wahunsunacock, better known as Chief Powhatan, was the mamanatowick, or paramount chief, of more than thirty tribes in the Powhatan Chiefdom. He had inherited six tribes and gained the rest through marriage alliances and coercion. Their land covered tidewater Virginia between the James and Potomac Rivers, a region they called Tsenacommacah, about 100 miles by 100 miles. The National Park Service estimates a population of at least 25,000 before English diseases, and about 15,000 in 1607.
pageData.para2: Each tribe had its own chief, a weroance or weroansqua, but all paid tribute to Powhatan. Encyclopedia.com adds that the confederacy had a peace chief for internal affairs, a war chief for external affairs and a council that included priests. In the winter of 1607 John Smith was taken to Werowocomoco, where Powhatan lived, and was released in the spring of 1608. Powhatan then sent food to the English, often with his daughter Pocahontas. After Smith left in 1609, relations soured and Powhatan moved inland to Orapaks.
pageData.para3: In 1613 the English kidnapped Pocahontas. In 1614 she married John Rolfe, and the marriage brought a peace known as the Peace of Pocahontas. She died in England in 1617, and Powhatan died in 1618. His brother Opechancanough took over. Tired of English expansion, he planned a coordinated attack in 1622 that killed about 350 to 400 of roughly 1,200 settlers, although Jamestown was spared after a warning. Conflict continued on and off. In 1644 Opechancanough led another attack, when the English population had grown to about 8,000.
pageData.para4: In 1646 the English captured Opechancanough, who was about 100, and a guard shot him. The National Park Service says his death began the end of the Powhatan Chiefdom. Treaties in 1646 and 1677 limited Indian access to land, set up reservations and, in 1677, required yearly tribute to the English king. The Mattaponi and Pamunkey still keep their reservations. In 1924 Virginia's Racial Integrity Act recognized only two racial categories, white and colored, and officials such as Walter Plecker used it to deny that Virginia Indians existed. The picture on this page is an imagined 19th-century likeness of Powhatan from an 1880 engraving, not a portrait made from life.
